<!-- def-1: body_md -->
\label{qus:def:sample-space}
    Throughout, the sample space is the \emph{universal Hilbert cube} of \cite[\S7]{For21}:
    \begin{align}
        \Omega &:= [0,1]^\mathbb{N}, &
        \mathcal{B}_\Omega &:= \left (  \textstyle\bigotimes_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{B}_{[0,1]}\right ) _\mathsf{u}, \\
        \Omega^\Omega &:= \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega)\right ) , &
        \mathsf{P}_\Omega &:= \mathcal{P}(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),
    \end{align}
    where $\mathcal{B}_\otimes := \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{B}_{[0,1]}$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of the
    cube and $(\cdot)_\mathsf{u}$ is universal completion, so that $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ consists of \emph{all}
    universally measurable subsets, $\Omega^\Omega$ is the monoid of all universally measurable
    self-maps, and $\mathsf{P}_\Omega$ is the set of all probability measures on $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$. We write
    $U := \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}U[0,1]$ for the uniform measure, and $\mathcal{P}(E,\mathcal{B}_E)$ for the set
    of all probability measures on an ordinary measurable space $(E,\mathcal{B}_E)$.
<!-- end def-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{qus:thm:omega-properties}
    The sample space of \Cref{qus:def:sample-space} has the following properties.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[($\Omega$1)] $\Omega^\Omega$ is a monoid under composition containing $\mathrm{id}_\Omega$ and
            all constant maps.
        \item[($\Omega$2)] \emph{Product isomorphism.} The zip-locker map
            $\Theta = (\Theta_1,\Theta_2):\,\Omega \stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \Omega\times\Omega$, which de-interleaves
            the coordinates of a sequence, is a Borel isomorphism; so
            $\Omega\times\Omega \cong \Omega$ and, iterating, $\Omega^\mathbb{N} \cong \Omega$. We write
            $\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$ for the inverse, so that
            $\Theta_1\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega') = \omega$ and
            $\Theta_2\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega') = \omega'$.
        \item[($\Omega$3)] \emph{Fubini property.} For $P_1,P_2 \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$ the two iterated
            integrals of a bounded $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$-measurable function agree, so that
            $P_1\otimes P_2$ is well defined on $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$ and symmetric. Here
            $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$ is the \emph{induced} $\sigma$-algebra of the
            quasi-universal product, \Cref{qus:def:induced-sigma} below; it is in general strictly
            larger than $\mathcal{B}_\Omega\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$, and the strength of ($\Omega$3) lies
            in that.
        \item[($\Omega$4)] \emph{Universal completeness.} $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ consists of all universally
            measurable sets; in particular it contains every analytic subset of $\Omega$.
        \item[($\Omega$5)] \emph{Universality.} $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\otimes)$ is standard Borel, every
            standard Borel space embeds into it with Borel image, $U$ is atomless, and for every
            $P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$ there is $\psi \in \Omega^\Omega$ with $\psi_*U = P$.
        \item[($\Omega$6)] $\mathsf{P}_\Omega$ consists of \emph{all} probability measures on $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$,
            so push-forwards may be taken freely.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{qus:lem:borel-suffices}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item A self-map of the cube is admissible as soon as it is Borel-measurable:
            \begin{align}
                \Omega^\Omega &= \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\otimes)\right )  .
                \nonumber
            \end{align}
        \item If $\Phi_1,\Phi_2 \in \Omega^\Omega$ then
            $\Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2) \in \Omega^\Omega$. Consequently
            $\Theta:\,\Omega\to\Omega\times\Omega$ is an isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces, and
            $A\mapsto\Theta(A)$ is a bijection $\mathcal{B}_\Omega \stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    \begin{proof}
        (1) ``$\subseteq$'' holds because $\mathcal{B}_\otimes \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\Omega$. For ``$\supseteq$'' let $f$ be
        Borel-measurable and let $S \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega$. For $P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$ the push-forward $f_*P$ is
        a Borel probability measure on the standard Borel space $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\otimes)$, and $S$ is
        universally measurable by ($\Omega$4), so there are $B_1 \subseteq S \subseteq B_2$ in $\mathcal{B}_\otimes$
        with $f_*P(B_2\setminus B_1) = 0$. Then $f^{-1}(B_1) \subseteq f^{-1}(S) \subseteq f^{-1}(B_2)$ with
        $P\left (  f^{-1}(B_2)\setminus f^{-1}(B_1)\right )  = 0$, so $f^{-1}(S)$ lies in the $P$-completion of
        $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$. As $P$ was arbitrary and $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is its own universal completion by
        ($\Omega$4), $f^{-1}(S) \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega$.

        (2) The rectangles $A_1\times A_2$ with $A_i \in \mathcal{B}_\otimes$ generate
        $\mathcal{B}_\otimes\otimes\mathcal{B}_\otimes$, and
        $(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)^{-1}(A_1\times A_2) = \Phi_1^{-1}(A_1)\cap\Phi_2^{-1}(A_2) \in
        \mathcal{B}_\Omega$; so $(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)$ is
        $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$-$(\mathcal{B}_\otimes\otimes\mathcal{B}_\otimes)$-measurable, and composing with the
        Borel map $\Theta^{-1}$ of ($\Omega$2) and applying (1) gives
        $\Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2) \in \Omega^\Omega$. Since $\Theta_1,\Theta_2$ are Borel,
        $\Theta$ is quasi-measurable, and what has just been shown says that its inverse is; an
        isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces induces a bijection of the induced $\sigma$-algebras
        of \Cref{qus:def:induced-sigma}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(1) ``$\subseteq$'' holds because $\mathcal{B}_\otimes \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\Omega$. For ``$\supseteq$'' let $f$ be
        Borel-measurable and let $S \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega$. For $P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$ the push-forward $f_*P$ is
        a Borel probability measure on the standard Borel space $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\otimes)$, and $S$ is
        universally measurable by ($\Omega$4), so there are $B_1 \subseteq S \subseteq B_2$ in $\mathcal{B}_\otimes$
        with $f_*P(B_2\setminus B_1) = 0$. Then $f^{-1}(B_1) \subseteq f^{-1}(S) \subseteq f^{-1}(B_2)$ with
        $P\left (  f^{-1}(B_2)\setminus f^{-1}(B_1)\right )  = 0$, so $f^{-1}(S)$ lies in the $P$-completion of
        $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$. As $P$ was arbitrary and $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is its own universal completion by
        ($\Omega$4), $f^{-1}(S) \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega$.

        (2) The rectangles $A_1\times A_2$ with $A_i \in \mathcal{B}_\otimes$ generate
        $\mathcal{B}_\otimes\otimes\mathcal{B}_\otimes$, and
        $(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)^{-1}(A_1\times A_2) = \Phi_1^{-1}(A_1)\cap\Phi_2^{-1}(A_2) \in
        \mathcal{B}_\Omega$; so $(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)$ is
        $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$-$(\mathcal{B}_\otimes\otimes\mathcal{B}_\otimes)$-measurable, and composing with the
        Borel map $\Theta^{-1}$ of ($\Omega$2) and applying (1) gives
        $\Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2) \in \Omega^\Omega$. Since $\Theta_1,\Theta_2$ are Borel,
        $\Theta$ is quasi-measurable, and what has just been shown says that its inverse is; an
        isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces induces a bijection of the induced $\sigma$-algebras
        of \Cref{qus:def:induced-sigma}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{qus:lem:split-U}
    $\Theta_*U = U\otimes U$. Under $U$ the two halves $\Theta_1,\Theta_2$ of a seed are
    independent and each is again uniform, so splitting a seed needs no auxiliary measure.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- def-2: body_md -->
\label{qus:def:qus}
    A \emph{quasi-universal space} $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}^\Omega)$ is a set $\mathcal{S}$ together with a set
    $\mathcal{S}^\Omega$ of maps $X:\,\Omega\to\mathcal{S}$, the \emph{admissible random variables}, containing
    all constant maps and satisfying $X\circ\Phi \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ for all $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ and
    $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$. A map $g:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{T}$ is \emph{quasi-measurable} if
    $g\circ X \in \mathcal{T}^\Omega$ for all $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$. The resulting category is $\mathbf{QUS}$, and
    $\mathcal{S}^\Omega = \mathbf{QUS}(\Omega,\mathcal{S})$.
<!-- end def-2 -->
<!-- def-3: body_md -->
\label{qus:def:induced-sigma}
    Put
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S} &:= \left \{  A \subseteq \mathcal{S} \,\middle|\, \forall X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega.\;
        X^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega \right \}  ,
    \end{align}
    the final $\sigma$-algebra of the family $\mathcal{S}^\Omega$. Every admissible random variable and
    every quasi-measurable map is measurable for these $\sigma$-algebras, and
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S} &= \bigcap_{X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega,\, P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega} X_*\left ( \mathcal{B}_\Omega\right ) _P ,
        \label{eq:induced-sigma-explicit}
    \end{align}
    so $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S}$ is universally complete. The inclusion
    $\mathcal{S}^\Omega \subseteq \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S})\right ) $ is in general strict.
<!-- end def-3 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{qus:thm:quasitopos}
    $\mathbf{QUS}$ is complete, cocomplete, cartesian closed and locally cartesian closed, and it is a
    quasitopos. Products and function spaces are
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \textstyle\prod_i\mathcal{S}_i\right ) ^\Omega &= \textstyle\prod_i \mathcal{S}_i^\Omega, &
        \left ( \mathcal{T}^\mathcal{S}\right ) ^\Omega &= \left \{  Y \,\middle|\, \forall \Phi \in \Omega^\Omega\ \forall X \in
        \mathcal{S}^\Omega.\ \left ( \omega\mapsto Y(\Phi(\omega))(X(\omega))\right )  \in \mathcal{T}^\Omega\right \}  ,
    \end{align}
    coproducts are \emph{rigid}, $\left ( \coprod_i\mathcal{S}_i\right ) ^\Omega = \bigcup_i\iota_i\circ
    \mathcal{S}_i^\Omega$, and the indiscrete two-point space ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ of \Cref{sss:eg:two} classifies
    embeddings.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- def-4: body_md -->
\label{qus:def:PrPf}
    For $\mathcal{S} \in \mathbf{QUS}$,
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{S}) &:= \left \{  X_*P \,\middle|\, X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega,\, P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega\right \}  \subseteq
        \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S}), \\
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{S})^\Omega &:= \left \{  \left ( \omega\mapsto X(\omega)_*P\right )  \,\middle|\,
        X \in \left ( \mathcal{S}^\Omega\right ) ^\Omega,\, P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega\right \}  .
    \end{align}
<!-- end def-4 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{qus:thm:PrPf}
    $(\mathsf{P},\delta,\mathbb{M})$, with $\delta_\mathcal{S}(x) := \delta_x$ and
    $\mathbb{M}_\mathcal{S}(\Gamma) := \int \nu\,\Gamma(d\nu)$, is a strong commutative affine monad on $\mathbf{QUS}$. The
    product of measures $\mu\otimes\nu$ is defined on all of $\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{T}}$, not merely
    on $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{T}$, by
    \begin{align}
        (\mu\otimes\nu)(C) &:= \int\!\!\int \mathds{1}\left [  \left (  X(\omega_1),Y(\omega_2)\right )  \in C \right ] 
        \, U(d\omega_2)\, U(d\omega_1), \qquad C \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{T}},
        \label{eq:otimes-section}
    \end{align}
    for any $X,Y$ with $X_*U = \mu$, $Y_*U = \nu$; the right-hand side is well defined by
    ($\Omega$3), independent of the choice of $X,Y$, and restricts to the usual product measure on
    $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{T}$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{qus:lem:caratheodory}
    Let $(A,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space, $T$ a separable metrizable space, $E$ a metrizable
    space, and $g:\,T\times A \to E$ a map which is continuous in the first argument for each fixed
    second argument and $\mathcal{A}$-measurable in the second for each fixed first. Then $g$ is
    $\mathcal{B}_T\otimes\mathcal{A}$-measurable, where $\mathcal{B}_T$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $T$.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $D \subseteq T$ be countable dense and, for $k \ge 1$, let $\left \{  T_{k,d}\right \} _{d \in D}$ be the
        Borel partition of $T$ obtained from the cover by the balls $B(d,1/k)$, $d\in D$, by
        disjointification along a fixed enumeration of $D$. Put
        $g_k(t,a) := g(d_k(t),a)$, where $d_k(t)$ is the unique $d$ with $t \in T_{k,d}$. Each
        $g_k$ is $\mathcal{B}_T\otimes\mathcal{A}$-measurable, being a countable ``staircase'': on
        $T_{k,d}\times A$ it equals the measurable map $g(d,-)$ composed with the projection.
        Since $d_k(t) \to t$ and $g$ is continuous in the first argument, $g_k \to g$ pointwise,
        and a pointwise limit of measurable maps into a metrizable space is measurable.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $D \subseteq T$ be countable dense and, for $k \ge 1$, let $\left \{  T_{k,d}\right \} _{d \in D}$ be the
        Borel partition of $T$ obtained from the cover by the balls $B(d,1/k)$, $d\in D$, by
        disjointification along a fixed enumeration of $D$. Put
        $g_k(t,a) := g(d_k(t),a)$, where $d_k(t)$ is the unique $d$ with $t \in T_{k,d}$. Each
        $g_k$ is $\mathcal{B}_T\otimes\mathcal{A}$-measurable, being a countable ``staircase'': on
        $T_{k,d}\times A$ it equals the measurable map $g(d,-)$ composed with the projection.
        Since $d_k(t) \to t$ and $g$ is continuous in the first argument, $g_k \to g$ pointwise,
        and a pointwise limit of measurable maps into a metrizable space is measurable.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- def-5: body_md -->
\label{site:def:site}
    Let $\mathbb{S}$ be the category with objects $\Omega_n$, $n \ge 0$, and with
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n) &:= \left \{  (g,\Phi) \,\middle|\, g \in \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n),\
        \Phi \in \Omega^\Omega \right \} , &
        (g,\Phi)(t,\omega) &:= \left (  g(t,\omega),\, \Phi(\omega)\right ) ,
    \end{align}
    where $\mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n)$, the set of \emph{mixed-smooth} maps, is the set of maps
    $g:\,\Omega_m = \mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(M1)] $g(-,\omega) \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$, and
        \item[(M2)] $g(t,-)$ is $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$-$\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}$-measurable for every
            $t \in \mathbb{R}^m$, where $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ is the \emph{Borel} $\sigma$-algebra.
    \end{enumerate}
    Note the asymmetry: the smooth component may depend on the seed, whereas the seed component
    $\Phi$ may \emph{not} depend on $t$. This is not a stipulation of convenience --- it is forced
    if $\mathbb{S}$ is to be a category at all, \Cref{site:rem:flat}.
<!-- end def-5 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{site:lem:category}
    Identities lie in $\mathbb{S}$ and composition of the maps above is again of the same form, so
    \Cref{site:def:site} defines a category, and every $\mathbb{S}$-morphism is in particular
    measurable from $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^m}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ to
    $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$.
    \begin{proof}
        For the identity take $g = \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ and $\Phi = \mathrm{id}_\Omega$. Let
        $(g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and $(g',\Phi') \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_n,\Omega_k)$. The
        composite is $(g'',\Phi'\circ\Phi)$ with
        $g''(t,\omega) = g'\left (  g(t,\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) $, and $\Phi'\circ\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$
        by ($\Omega$1). For (M1), fix $\omega$: $g(-,\omega)$ is $C^\infty$ and
        $g'(-,\Phi(\omega))$ is $C^\infty$, so the composite is $C^\infty$. For (M2), fix $t$: by
        \Cref{qus:lem:caratheodory} applied to $g'$ --- which is continuous in the first argument by
        (M1) and measurable in the second by (M2) --- the map $g'$ is
        $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$-measurable; and
        $\omega \mapsto \left (  g(t,\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) $ is measurable into
        $\left ( \mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega,\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega\right ) $ by (M2) for $g$ and by
        $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$. The composite of the two is measurable. Associativity and the unit
        laws are inherited from composition of maps. The last claim is
        \Cref{qus:lem:caratheodory} again.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For the identity take $g = \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ and $\Phi = \mathrm{id}_\Omega$. Let
        $(g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and $(g',\Phi') \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_n,\Omega_k)$. The
        composite is $(g'',\Phi'\circ\Phi)$ with
        $g''(t,\omega) = g'\left (  g(t,\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) $, and $\Phi'\circ\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$
        by ($\Omega$1). For (M1), fix $\omega$: $g(-,\omega)$ is $C^\infty$ and
        $g'(-,\Phi(\omega))$ is $C^\infty$, so the composite is $C^\infty$. For (M2), fix $t$: by
        \Cref{qus:lem:caratheodory} applied to $g'$ --- which is continuous in the first argument by
        (M1) and measurable in the second by (M2) --- the map $g'$ is
        $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$-measurable; and
        $\omega \mapsto \left (  g(t,\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) $ is measurable into
        $\left ( \mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega,\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega\right ) $ by (M2) for $g$ and by
        $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$. The composite of the two is measurable. Associativity and the unit
        laws are inherited from composition of maps. The last claim is
        \Cref{qus:lem:caratheodory} again.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- not-1: body_md -->
\label{site:not:morphisms}
    We name the substitutions used throughout. Let $n,m \ge 0$.
    \begin{align}
        \pi_n &:= (\,!\,,\mathrm{id}_\Omega):\; \Omega_n \to \Omega_0, &
        \pi_n(t,\omega) &= \omega, \\
        \iota^n_{t_0} &:= (t_0,\mathrm{id}_\Omega):\; \Omega_0 \to \Omega_n, &
        \iota^n_{t_0}(\omega) &= (t_0,\omega), \\
        \left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle  &:= (W,\Phi):\; \Omega_0 \to \Omega_n, &
        \left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle (\omega) &= \left (  W(\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) , \\
        \Xi^{(n)} &:= (\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\Xi):\; \Omega_n \to \Omega_n, &
        \Xi^{(n)}(t,\omega) &= \left (  t,\Xi(\omega)\right ) , \\
        \varphi^{(n)} &:= (\varphi\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m},\mathrm{id}_\Omega):\; \Omega_m \to \Omega_n, &
        \varphi^{(n)}(t,\omega) &= \left ( \varphi(t),\omega\right ) ,
    \end{align}
    for $W \in \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n})\right ) $,
    $\Phi,\Xi \in \Omega^\Omega$, $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$
    and $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n)$. All five are $\mathbb{S}$-morphisms. The third, in which the
    smooth coordinate is read off the seed, is the \emph{mixed} morphism of
    \Cref{site:rem:mixed}; it exists only because the target carries both directions, and it has no
    counterpart if the two directions are kept apart.
<!-- end not-1 -->
<!-- prp-1: body_md -->
\label{site:prp:products}
    For $m,n \ge 0$ the object $\Omega_{m+n}$, together with
    \begin{align}
        q_1 &:= \left (  \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m}\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^{m+n}},\ \Theta_1 \right ) :\; \Omega_{m+n} \to \Omega_m, &
        q_2 &:= \left (  \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^{m+n}},\ \Theta_2 \right ) :\; \Omega_{m+n} \to \Omega_n,
    \end{align}
    where $\mathbb{R}^{m+n} = \mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Theta = (\Theta_1,\Theta_2)$ is the isomorphism of
    ($\Omega$2), is a product of $\Omega_m$ and $\Omega_n$ in $\mathbb{S}$. Consequently $\mathbb{S}$ has all
    finite non-empty products. It has \emph{no} terminal object: $\mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_0) = \Omega^\Omega$ has more than
    one element, and for $n \ge 1$ so does $\mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$, which contains the distinct
    morphisms $\iota^n_{t_0}$, $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$.
    \begin{proof}
        $q_1,q_2$ are $\mathbb{S}$-morphisms, their smooth parts being linear projections and their seed
        parts lying in $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$2) together with
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(1). Let $f_i = (g_i,\Phi_i) \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{n_i})$ for $(n_1,n_2) = (m,n)$. A morphism
        $h = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{m+n})$ satisfies $q_i \circ h = f_i$ if and only if
        $g = (g_1,g_2)$ and $\Theta_i\circ\Phi = \Phi_i$, i.e.\ $\Phi = \Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)$.
        This determines $h$ uniquely; and $h$ is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism, since $(g_1,g_2)$ satisfies
        (M1) and (M2) componentwise and $\Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2) \in \Omega^\Omega$ by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2).
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$q_1,q_2$ are $\mathbb{S}$-morphisms, their smooth parts being linear projections and their seed
        parts lying in $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$2) together with
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(1). Let $f_i = (g_i,\Phi_i) \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{n_i})$ for $(n_1,n_2) = (m,n)$. A morphism
        $h = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{m+n})$ satisfies $q_i \circ h = f_i$ if and only if
        $g = (g_1,g_2)$ and $\Theta_i\circ\Phi = \Phi_i$, i.e.\ $\Phi = \Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2)$.
        This determines $h$ uniquely; and $h$ is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism, since $(g_1,g_2)$ satisfies
        (M1) and (M2) componentwise and $\Theta^{-1}(\Phi_1,\Phi_2) \in \Omega^\Omega$ by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- def-6: body_md -->
\label{site:def:site-plus}
    Let $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ have objects $\Omega_n$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 0$, with $\mathbb{R}^0 = \ast$ the one-point
    space, and morphisms
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\Omega_n) &:= \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n), &
        \mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n) &:= \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n), \\
        \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n) &:= C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n), &
        \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\Omega_n) &:= C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n) \times \Omega ,
    \end{align}
    the last being the pairs $(\varphi,\omega_0)$ giving $t \mapsto (\varphi(t),\omega_0)$, so that
    a map into the seed direction out of a purely smooth object is constant. Composition is
    composition of maps, and that it is well defined is checked case by case: the two purely mixed
    cases are \Cref{site:lem:category}; the cases $\Omega_m\to\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and
    $\mathbb{R}^m\to\Omega_n\to\mathbb{R}^k$ use (M1), (M2) and the chain rule; $\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$ is
    composition of $C^\infty$ maps; and in the three remaining cases, all with target $\Omega_k$,
    the seed component of the composite is a constant, $\omega\mapsto\Phi'(\omega_0)$ resp.\
    $\omega\mapsto\omega_0$, which lies in $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$1).
<!-- end def-6 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{site:lem:products-plus}
    In $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ the object $\ast = \mathbb{R}^0$ is terminal, and binary products exist:
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n &= \mathbb{R}^{m+n}, &
        \mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega_n &= \Omega_{m+n}, &
        \Omega_m\times\Omega_n &\;\cong\; \Omega_{m+n},
        \label{eq:site-plus-products}
    \end{align}
    the first two with the projections of the underlying sets, under the usual identifications
    $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ and $\mathbb{R}^m\times\left ( \mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega\right )  =
    \mathbb{R}^{m+n}\times\Omega$. Only the third requires the zip-locker isomorphism $\Theta$, and it is
    an isomorphism rather than an equality for that reason.
    \begin{proof}
        $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\ast) = \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^0)$ and $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\ast) =
        C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^0)$ are singletons, so $\ast$ is terminal.

        For $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$: the two projections are smooth. A cone from $\mathbb{R}^k$ is a
        pair $\varphi_i \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^{n_i})$ and factors uniquely through
        $(\varphi_1,\varphi_2) \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^{m+n})$; a cone from $\Omega_k$ is a pair
        $f_i \in \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^{n_i})$ and factors uniquely through $(f_1,f_2)$, which lies in
        $\mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^{m+n})$ because (M1) and (M2) are conditions on the components.

        For $\mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega_n = \Omega_{m+n}$: the projections are $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m} \in
        \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_{m+n},\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\mathrm{id}_\Omega\right )  \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_{m+n},\Omega_n)$, where $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m},\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ are taken on the
        $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ factor. A cone from $\Omega_k$ is a pair $f_1 \in \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^m)$ and
        $f_2 = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_n)$, and $h = (\tilde g,\tilde\Phi) \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{m+n})$ makes both triangles commute if and only if
        $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m}\circ\tilde g = f_1$, $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\circ\tilde g = g$ and
        $\tilde\Phi = \Phi$, that is $h = \left (  (f_1,g),\Phi\right ) $, which is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        because (M1) and (M2) hold componentwise. A cone from $\mathbb{R}^k$ is a pair
        $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $(\psi,\omega_0) \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^k,\Omega_n)$,
        and factors uniquely through $\left ( (\varphi,\psi),\omega_0\right ) $. Note that the seed is
        \emph{not} duplicated here, because $\mathbb{R}^m$ carries none; this is why no $\Theta$ appears
        and the product is the object $\Omega_{m+n}$ on the nose.

        For $\Omega_m\times\Omega_n \cong \Omega_{m+n}$: the cone of \Cref{site:prp:products}
        already has the universal property against the test objects $\Omega_k$. Against $\mathbb{R}^k$, a
        cone is a pair $(\varphi_i,\omega_i) \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^k,\Omega_{n_i})$, and
        $q_i\circ(\varphi,\omega_0) = \left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^{n_i}}\circ\varphi,\ \Theta_i\omega_0\right ) $,
        so the unique factorisation is
        $\left ( (\varphi_1,\varphi_2),\ \Theta^{-1}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\right ) $.

        Finite products now follow, the empty one being $\ast$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
$\mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\ast) = \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^0)$ and $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\ast) =
        C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^0)$ are singletons, so $\ast$ is terminal.

        For $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$: the two projections are smooth. A cone from $\mathbb{R}^k$ is a
        pair $\varphi_i \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^{n_i})$ and factors uniquely through
        $(\varphi_1,\varphi_2) \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^{m+n})$; a cone from $\Omega_k$ is a pair
        $f_i \in \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^{n_i})$ and factors uniquely through $(f_1,f_2)$, which lies in
        $\mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^{m+n})$ because (M1) and (M2) are conditions on the components.

        For $\mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega_n = \Omega_{m+n}$: the projections are $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m} \in
        \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_{m+n},\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\mathrm{id}_\Omega\right )  \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_{m+n},\Omega_n)$, where $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m},\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ are taken on the
        $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ factor. A cone from $\Omega_k$ is a pair $f_1 \in \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_k,\mathbb{R}^m)$ and
        $f_2 = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_n)$, and $h = (\tilde g,\tilde\Phi) \in
        \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_{m+n})$ makes both triangles commute if and only if
        $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m}\circ\tilde g = f_1$, $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\circ\tilde g = g$ and
        $\tilde\Phi = \Phi$, that is $h = \left (  (f_1,g),\Phi\right ) $, which is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        because (M1) and (M2) hold componentwise. A cone from $\mathbb{R}^k$ is a pair
        $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^m)$ and $(\psi,\omega_0) \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^k,\Omega_n)$,
        and factors uniquely through $\left ( (\varphi,\psi),\omega_0\right ) $. Note that the seed is
        \emph{not} duplicated here, because $\mathbb{R}^m$ carries none; this is why no $\Theta$ appears
        and the product is the object $\Omega_{m+n}$ on the nose.

        For $\Omega_m\times\Omega_n \cong \Omega_{m+n}$: the cone of \Cref{site:prp:products}
        already has the universal property against the test objects $\Omega_k$. Against $\mathbb{R}^k$, a
        cone is a pair $(\varphi_i,\omega_i) \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^k,\Omega_{n_i})$, and
        $q_i\circ(\varphi,\omega_0) = \left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^{n_i}}\circ\varphi,\ \Theta_i\omega_0\right ) $,
        so the unique factorisation is
        $\left ( (\varphi_1,\varphi_2),\ \Theta^{-1}(\omega_1,\omega_2)\right ) $.

        Finite products now follow, the empty one being $\ast$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prp-2: body_md -->
\label{site:prp:retracts}
    Fix $\omega_0 \in \Omega$ and let
    \begin{align}
        \iota &:= (\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\omega_0):\; \mathbb{R}^n \to \Omega_n, &
        \pi &:= \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}:\; \Omega_n \to \mathbb{R}^n .
    \end{align}
    Then $\pi\circ\iota = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, and $e := \iota\circ\pi \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_n,\Omega_n)$,
    $e(t,\omega) = (t,\omega_0)$, is an idempotent of $\mathbb{S}$ whose splitting is $\mathbb{R}^n$. In
    particular $\ast = \mathbb{R}^0$ splits the idempotent $\omega\mapsto\omega_0$ of $\Omega_0$.
<!-- end prp-2 -->
<!-- prp-3: body_md -->
\label{site:prp:karoubi}
    Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a set and let $\left ( \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}\right ) _{n\ge0}$ be families of maps
    $\Omega_n \to \mathcal{X}$ containing the constants and closed under precomposition with
    $\mathbb{S}$-morphisms. Then there is exactly one way to extend them to families
    $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ closed under precomposition with $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphisms, namely
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n} &= \left \{  \gamma:\,\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathcal{X} \,\middle|\, \gamma\circ\pi \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} \right \}  ,
        \label{eq:karoubi}
    \end{align}
    and it satisfies $\mathcal{X}^\ast = \mathcal{X}$. Consequently the categories of such structures over
    $\mathbb{S}$ and over $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ are isomorphic.
    \begin{proof}
        Suppose the families are given and closed. If $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ then
        $\gamma\circ\pi \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, since $\pi$ is a $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphism; this is
        ``$\subseteq$'' in \Cref{eq:karoubi}. Conversely if $\gamma\circ\pi \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ then,
        $\iota$ being a $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphism,
        $\gamma = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ\iota \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, which is ``$\supseteq$''. So the
        extension is unique if it exists.

        For existence, define $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ by \Cref{eq:karoubi} and check closure. Let
        $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$. For $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n)$,
        $(\gamma\circ\varphi)\circ\pi = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ\varphi^{(n)} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ by
        \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, so $\gamma\circ\varphi \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^m}$. For
        $g \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ we must show $\gamma\circ g \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$: indeed
        $(g,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and
        $\gamma\circ g = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ(g,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$. Closure of
        $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ under $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\Omega_n)$ and $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ is
        immediate from \Cref{eq:karoubi} and the hypothesis. Finally
        $\mathcal{X}^\ast = \left \{  x \,\middle|\, \mathrm{const}_x \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right \}  = \mathcal{X}$ because constants
        are plots.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose the families are given and closed. If $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ then
        $\gamma\circ\pi \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, since $\pi$ is a $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphism; this is
        ``$\subseteq$'' in \Cref{eq:karoubi}. Conversely if $\gamma\circ\pi \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ then,
        $\iota$ being a $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphism,
        $\gamma = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ\iota \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, which is ``$\supseteq$''. So the
        extension is unique if it exists.

        For existence, define $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ by \Cref{eq:karoubi} and check closure. Let
        $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$. For $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n)$,
        $(\gamma\circ\varphi)\circ\pi = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ\varphi^{(n)} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ by
        \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, so $\gamma\circ\varphi \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^m}$. For
        $g \in \mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ we must show $\gamma\circ g \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$: indeed
        $(g,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and
        $\gamma\circ g = (\gamma\circ\pi)\circ(g,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$. Closure of
        $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ under $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\mathbb{R}^m,\Omega_n)$ and $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ is
        immediate from \Cref{eq:karoubi} and the hypothesis. Finally
        $\mathcal{X}^\ast = \left \{  x \,\middle|\, \mathrm{const}_x \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right \}  = \mathcal{X}$ because constants
        are plots.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
\label{site:rem:mixed}
    Since \Cref{site:prp:karoubi} says the purely smooth test objects add no plots, one may ask what
    putting $\Omega$ into every test object is for. The answer is
    $\left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle  \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$ of \Cref{site:not:morphisms}: the substitution in
    which the smooth coordinate is itself read off the seed. Two consequences, both structural.

    First, closure of plot families under $\left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle $ says that a smooth family is
    automatically measurable: if $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_1}$ and $W$ is a measurable real random
    variable, then $\omega\mapsto p(W(\omega),\omega)$ is an admissible random variable. In a theory
    built on two disjoint families of maps out of $\mathbb{R}$ and out of $\Omega$ this is not available
    and has to be imposed as an axiom; here it is an instance of closure.

    Second, and this is what \Cref{sec:prob} lives on, the mixed plot family
    $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ is \emph{primitive data} rather than something computed from $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$
    and the curves. This is the obstruction set out as (a), (b), (c) in \Cref{sec:intro}: with two
    separate families, conditions (a) and (b) --- smooth for each seed, admissible under each
    substitution --- are all one can state of a family of measures, whereas the multiplication of
    \Cref{prob:thm:mult} consumes (c), the existence of a single representative $Y$; and getting (c)
    from (a) and (b) is a measurable selection problem whose solvability we do not know,
    \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}. Put differently, with two families the mixed data is
    \emph{forced} to be an internal hom, whereas the monad needs it to be a push-forward image. Over
    the present site (c) is simply a plot condition, and \Cref{prob:def:PrPf} takes it as the
    definition: the mixed family is ours to choose, and that is the whole of the difference.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
\label{site:rem:flat}
    The seed component $\Phi$ of a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism is required to be independent of $t$. This is
    the statement that $\Omega$ carries no smooth structure, and it is forced: were $\Phi$ allowed
    to depend on $t$, subject only to a measurability condition in $\omega$ --- there being no
    smooth structure on $\Omega$ to constrain it --- then $\mathbb{S}$ would not be a category, because
    (M1) would not survive composition. For a witness take $m=n=k=1$, $g := \mathrm{pr}_\mathbb{R}$ and
    $\Phi(t,\omega) := \left ( \tfrac{|t|}{1+|t|},0,0,\dots\right )  \in \Omega$, each of whose sections at
    fixed $t$ is constant in $\omega$ and hence measurable, together with
    $g'(s,\omega') := \omega'_0$, the first coordinate, which is Borel; the composite has smooth
    part $g''(t,\omega) = |t|/(1+|t|)$, which is not differentiable at $t = 0$, violating (M1). It is also why
    $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ is an acceptable sample space although it is neither a manifold nor without
    boundary: nothing smooth is ever asked of it.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
\label{site:rem:no-locality}
    Three omissions are deliberate.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item \emph{No open domains.} We do not include test objects $V\times\Omega$ for open
            $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Unlike $\mathbb{R}^n$ these are not retracts of objects of $\mathbb{S}$: a
            retraction $V\times\Omega\to\Omega_m\to V\times\Omega$, for any $m \ge 0$,
            restricts at each fixed seed to smooth maps exhibiting $V$ as a smooth retract of
            $\mathbb{R}^m$, and an annulus is a retract of no $\mathbb{R}^m$, since a retract of a contractible
            space has vanishing $H^1$. So
            this is a genuine restriction, not an application of \Cref{site:prp:karoubi}.
        \item \emph{No Grothendieck topology.} We use the trivial topology, for which every
            presheaf is a sheaf, so there is no sheaf condition and no gluing. Plot families are not
            required to be local in $t$.
        \item \emph{No patching in the seed direction.} As in \cite{For21} we do not require
            $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ to be closed under gluing along countable measurable partitions of
            $\Omega$; see \cite{HKSY17} for the variant that does.
    \end{enumerate}
    Items (1) and (2) go together and are discussed in \Cref{disc:rem:locality}: locality would buy
    gluing, which is what differential-geometric constructions on non-manifold objects need, and
    would cost the identification of $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$ with an image, which is what
    \Cref{sec:prob} needs.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
\label{site:rem:literature}
    Concrete sheaves on a concrete site are the standard machinery for convenient categories of
    smooth spaces, \cite{BH11,Dub79}, and \cite{MMS22} develops the $\omega$-concrete version with
    worked sites for standard Borel spaces, for Cartesian spaces and for piecewise-analytic
    domains. When \cite{MMS22} combines two such sites it does so by a \emph{sum}, identifying
    terminal and initial objects and adjoining constant maps between them; the resulting objects
    carry two independent plot families related only by constants, which is precisely the shape a
    presentation by curves and random variables would have. The present site is a \emph{product}:
    its
    objects mix the two directions, and by \Cref{site:rem:mixed} that is where all the difference
    lies. We are not aware of this instance in the literature, although the framework of
    \cite{BH11,Dub79,MMS22} accommodates it without modification.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- def-7: body_md -->
\label{sss:def:sample-smooth}
    A \emph{sample-smooth space} is a set $\mathcal{X}$ together with, for every $n \ge 0$, a set
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} &\subseteq \mathbf{Sets}\left ( \Omega_n,\ \mathcal{X}\right ) 
    \end{align}
    of \emph{admissible plots}, such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(P1)] every constant map $\Omega_n\to\mathcal{X}$ lies in $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$;
        \item[(P2)] $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ imply
            $p \circ h \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    A map $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ between sample-smooth spaces is \emph{sample-smooth} if
    $f\circ p \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$ for every $n$ and every $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. The resulting category is
    $\mathbf{SSS}$.
<!-- end def-7 -->
<!-- not-2: body_md -->
\label{sss:not:derived}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ we write
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{X}^\Omega &:= \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_0}, &
        \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n} &:= \left \{  \gamma:\,\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathcal{X} \,\middle|\, \gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}\right \} , &
        \mathcal{X}^\mathbb{R} &:= \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^1},
    \end{align}
    the \emph{admissible random variables}, the \emph{admissible $n$-parameter families} and the
    \emph{admissible curves}; by \Cref{site:prp:karoubi} these are the plot sets at the retracts
    $\mathbb{R}^n$ of $\Omega_n$, and $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^0} = \mathcal{X}$. Throughout, $\mathbb{R}^n$ denotes the Cartesian space
    of \Cref{sss:eg:euclidean} when it is used as a shape and its underlying set, vector space or
    Borel space when it is not; the reading is always fixed by the position, and the one place where
    the difference is substantive --- the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ against the
    induced one $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ --- is marked by the superscript $\circ$. We write
    $\natural\mathcal{X} := \left ( \mathcal{X},\mathcal{X}^\Omega\right ) $, a quasi-universal space by (P1) and by closure under
    $\Xi^{(0)} = \Xi$, and $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{X} := \mathcal{B}_{\natural\mathcal{X}}$ for its induced $\sigma$-algebra,
    \Cref{qus:def:induced-sigma}.
<!-- end not-2 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{sss:lem:Q4}
    Let $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ and $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, let
    $W \in \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n})\right ) $
    and let $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$. Then $\left ( \omega\mapsto\gamma(W(\omega))\right )  \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$, and
    more generally $\left ( \omega\mapsto p\left (  W(\omega),\Phi(\omega)\right ) \right )  \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ for every
    $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$.
    \begin{proof}
        The second statement is (P2) for the mixed morphism $\left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle $ of
        \Cref{site:not:morphisms}; the first is the second applied to
        $p := \gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The second statement is (P2) for the mixed morphism $\left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle $ of
        \Cref{site:not:morphisms}; the first is the second applied to
        $p := \gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}
    Give $\Omega_n$ the plot structure $\Omega_n^{\Omega_m} := \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$. This is a
    sample-smooth space, and for every $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} &= \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \Omega_n,\mathcal{X}\right ) , &
        \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n} &= \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{X}\right ) ,
    \end{align}
    the second with $\mathbb{R}^n$ the Cartesian space of \Cref{sss:eg:euclidean}. Moreover
    $p(-,\omega_0) \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ for every $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and every
    $\omega_0 \in \Omega$.
    \begin{proof}
        (P1) holds because a constant map $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ is the $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        $(\mathrm{const}_{t_0},\mathrm{const}_{\omega_0})$, and (P2) is composition in $\mathbb{S}$,
        \Cref{site:lem:category}. If $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\Omega_n,\mathcal{X})$ then
        $f = f\circ\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, since $\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_n} \in \Omega_n^{\Omega_n}$; and if
        $f \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ then $f\circ h \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ for every $h \in \Omega_n^{\Omega_m}$ by (P2), so
        $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\Omega_n,\mathcal{X})$.

        For the second equality, let $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, so
        $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ by \Cref{sss:not:derived}. If
        $q \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^{\Omega_m} = \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ then $(q,\mathrm{id}_\Omega)$ is a
        $\mathbb{S}$-morphism $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ and
        $\gamma\circ q = (\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n})\circ(q,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$,
        so $\gamma \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{X})$; conversely $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^{\Omega_n}$, so a
        sample-smooth $\gamma$ has $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. The last claim
        is (P2) applied to the $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        $(\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\mathrm{const}_{\omega_0}):\,\Omega_n\to\Omega_n$, whose seed part lies in
        $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$1), followed by \Cref{sss:not:derived}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(P1) holds because a constant map $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ is the $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        $(\mathrm{const}_{t_0},\mathrm{const}_{\omega_0})$, and (P2) is composition in $\mathbb{S}$,
        \Cref{site:lem:category}. If $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\Omega_n,\mathcal{X})$ then
        $f = f\circ\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, since $\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_n} \in \Omega_n^{\Omega_n}$; and if
        $f \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ then $f\circ h \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ for every $h \in \Omega_n^{\Omega_m}$ by (P2), so
        $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\Omega_n,\mathcal{X})$.

        For the second equality, let $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, so
        $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ by \Cref{sss:not:derived}. If
        $q \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^{\Omega_m} = \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ then $(q,\mathrm{id}_\Omega)$ is a
        $\mathbb{S}$-morphism $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ and
        $\gamma\circ q = (\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n})\circ(q,\mathrm{id}_\Omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$,
        so $\gamma \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{X})$; conversely $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^{\Omega_n}$, so a
        sample-smooth $\gamma$ has $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. The last claim
        is (P2) applied to the $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        $(\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\mathrm{const}_{\omega_0}):\,\Omega_n\to\Omega_n$, whose seed part lies in
        $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$1), followed by \Cref{sss:not:derived}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- eg-1: body_md -->
\label{sss:eg:euclidean}
    $\mathbb{R}^k$ carries $\left ( \mathbb{R}^k\right ) ^{\Omega_n} := \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_n,\mathbb{R}^k)$ of \Cref{site:def:site}, a plot
    structure by \Cref{site:lem:category}. Then $(\mathbb{R}^k)^\Omega = \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^k})\right ) $ is the set of
    \emph{universally measurable} maps $\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^k$ --- for which, by the argument of
    \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(1), it makes no difference whether one asks measurability into
    $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^k}$ or into its universal completion --- $(\mathbb{R}^k)^{\mathbb{R}^n} = C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}^k)$, and
    the induced $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k}$ of \Cref{sss:not:derived} is the universal
    completion of $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^k}$: ``$\supseteq$'' because a universally measurable set has
    universally measurable preimage under a universally measurable map, and ``$\subseteq$'' because, by
    ($\Omega$5), there is a Borel isomorphism $j$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$ onto a Borel subset of $\Omega$; its
    inverse, extended by a constant, is a Borel and hence admissible $X \in (\mathbb{R}^k)^\Omega$, and an
    arbitrary Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$ gives $P := j_*\mu \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$. For
    $A \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k}$ the set $X^{-1}(A)$ is $P$-measurable, and pulling a Borel sandwich back
    along $j$ exhibits $A$ as $\mu$-measurable. Note that the
    site could not have been phrased with $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^k}$ in place of $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^k}$: the
    induced $\sigma$-algebra is defined from the plot structure, which is defined from the site.
    We call $\mathbb{R}^k$ with this structure the \emph{Cartesian space} of dimension $k$. Further, $\mathbf{1}$ is the one-point space and $\mathbf{0}$ the empty one.
<!-- end eg-1 -->
<!-- eg-2: body_md -->
\label{sss:eg:two}
    On $\left \{ 0,1\right \} $ we use
    \begin{align}
        \breve{\mathbf{2}}^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{ \text{constants}\right \} , &
        {\text{\b{$\mathbf{2}$}}}^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{  \mathds{1}_B \,\middle|\, B \in \mathcal{B}_{\Omega_n} \right \} , &
        {\bar{\mathbf{2}}}^{\Omega_n} &:= \mathbf{Sets}\left ( \Omega_n,\left \{ 0,1\right \} \right ) ,
    \end{align}
    the \emph{constant}, the \emph{discrete} and the \emph{indiscrete} two-point space, where
    $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega_n}$ is the induced $\sigma$-algebra of the object $\Omega_n$ of
    \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}. Each is a plot structure; for ${\text{\b{$\mathbf{2}$}}}$ this is because a
    $\mathbb{S}$-morphism is sample-smooth, hence measurable for the induced $\sigma$-algebras. Note that
    $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega_n}$ is universally complete by \Cref{eq:induced-sigma-explicit} and contains the
    plain product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}^\circ_{\mathbb{R}^n}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ that
    \Cref{site:lem:category} delivers; the latter is used only as a generating family inside
    proofs.
<!-- end eg-2 -->
<!-- eg-3: body_md -->
\label{sss:eg:flat-sharp}
    For a quasi-universal space $\mathcal{S}$ put
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{  X \circ \pi_n \,\middle|\, X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega\right \} , &
        \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{  p \,\middle|\, \forall h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n).\ p \circ h \in
        \mathcal{S}^\Omega \right \}  .
    \end{align}
    Both are plot structures. $\flat\mathcal{S}$ has only the plots that ignore the smooth
    coordinate --- it is \emph{smoothly rigid}, $\flat\mathcal{S}^{\mathbb{R}^n} = $ constants --- and
    $\sharp\mathcal{S}$ has every plot that is compatible with the seed direction. These are the two
    modalities of \Cref{sec:modal}.
<!-- end eg-3 -->
<!-- eg-4: body_md -->
\label{sss:eg:manifolds}
    A finite-dimensional smooth manifold $M$, second-countable and Hausdorff, carries
    \begin{align}
        M^{\Omega_n} &:= \Big\{\, p:\,\Omega_n\to M \ \Big|\ p(-,\omega) \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,M)
        \text{ for all } \omega, \nonumber \\
        &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\ \
        p(t,-) \in \mathbf{Meas}\left ( (\Omega,\mathcal{B}_\Omega),(M,\mathcal{B}_M)\right )  \text{ for all } t \,\Big\},
        \label{eq:manifold-plots}
    \end{align}
    with $\mathcal{B}_M$ the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. We refer to the two conditions as (M1$_M$) and
    (M2$_M$); for $M = \mathbb{R}^k$ they are (M1) and (M2) of \Cref{site:def:site}. This is a plot structure: (P1) is clear, and for (P2)
    argue as in \Cref{site:lem:category}, using \Cref{qus:lem:caratheodory} for the metrizable
    target $M$.
<!-- end eg-4 -->
<!-- def-8: body_md -->
\label{sss:def:concrete-site}
    A \emph{concrete site} is a site $(\mathcal{E},J)$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(C1)] $\mathcal{E}$ has a terminal object $\ast$;
        \item[(C2)] the functor $|\cdot| := \mathcal{E}(\ast,-):\,\mathcal{E}\to\mathbf{Sets}$ is faithful;
        \item[(C3)] for every covering family $\left \{  f_i:\,C_i\to C\right \} _{i\in I} \in J(C)$ the maps
            $|f_i|$ are jointly surjective onto $|C|$.
    \end{enumerate}
    A presheaf $F$ on $\mathcal{E}$ is \emph{concrete} if for every object $C$ the map
    \begin{align}
        F(C) &\longrightarrow \mathbf{Sets}\left ( |C|,\ F(\ast)\right ) , &
        u &\longmapsto \left (  c \mapsto F(c)(u) \right ) ,
    \end{align}
    is injective. We write $\mathbf{cPsh}(\mathcal{E},J)$ for the full subcategory of concrete sheaves.
<!-- end def-8 -->
<!-- prp-4: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:concrete-site}
    Let $J_{\mathrm{triv}}$ be the trivial topology, whose only covering families are the singletons
    $\left \{ \mathrm{id}_C\right \} $. Then $(\mathbb{S}_\ast,J_{\mathrm{triv}})$ is a concrete site, every presheaf on it is
    a sheaf, and
    \begin{align}
        |\Omega_n| &= \mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega, & |\mathbb{R}^n| &= \mathbb{R}^n, & |\ast| &= \ast .
    \end{align}
    \begin{proof}
        (C1) $\ast = \mathbb{R}^0$ is terminal, \Cref{site:lem:products-plus}.

        (C2) $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\ast,\Omega_n) = C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^0,\mathbb{R}^n)\times\Omega = \mathbb{R}^n\times\Omega$ and
        $\mathbb{S}_\ast(\ast,\mathbb{R}^n) = \mathbb{R}^n$, and under these identifications $|f|$ is the underlying map of
        $f$. Since the morphisms of $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ \emph{are} maps of the underlying sets, $|\cdot|$
        is faithful.

        (C3) is vacuous for singleton covers by identities, and for the same reason every presheaf
        satisfies the sheaf condition.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-4 -->

        satisfies the sheaf condition.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- prp-5: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:sss-is-cpsh}
    $\mathbf{SSS} \cong \mathbf{cPsh}\left ( \mathbb{S}_\ast,J_{\mathrm{triv}}\right ) $.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $F$ be a concrete presheaf, $\mathcal{X} := F(\ast)$, and identify $F(C)$ with a subset of
        $\mathbf{Sets}(|C|,\mathcal{X})$ by (C2) and concreteness. Functoriality says exactly that these subsets
        are closed under precomposition with $\mathbb{S}_\ast$-morphisms, and for $x \in \mathcal{X}$ the
        element $F(!_C)(x) \in F(C)$ has underlying map $c \mapsto F(c)F(!_C)(x) = F(!_C\circ c)(x)
        = x$, the constant, so (P1) holds. Restricting to the objects $\Omega_n$ gives a
        sample-smooth space by \Cref{sss:def:sample-smooth}, and by \Cref{site:prp:karoubi} the values at
        $\mathbb{R}^n$ are recovered from it. Conversely a sample-smooth space extends uniquely to
        $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ by \Cref{eq:karoubi}, and the extension is a concrete presheaf. Morphisms
        correspond on both sides to maps of underlying sets commuting with the structure.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-5 -->

        $\mathbb{R}^n$ are recovered from it. Conversely a sample-smooth space extends uniquely to
        $\mathbb{S}_\ast$ by \Cref{eq:karoubi}, and the extension is a concrete presheaf. Morphisms
        correspond on both sides to maps of underlying sets commuting with the structure.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{sss:thm:quasitopos}
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ is a concrete quasitopos: it is complete and cocomplete, cartesian closed and locally
    cartesian closed, and the indiscrete two-point space ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ of \Cref{sss:eg:two} classifies
    strong monomorphisms. It is not a topos.
    \begin{proof}
        By \Cref{sss:prp:concrete-site,sss:prp:sss-is-cpsh}, $\mathbf{SSS}$ is the category of
        concrete sheaves on a concrete site, which is a quasitopos by \cite{BH11}; see also
        \cite{Dub79} and, for the version with additional structure, \cite{MMS22}. The explicit
        constructions, and direct verifications of completeness, cocompleteness, cartesian
        closedness and the classifier, are given in \Cref{sss:sec:constructions,sss:sec:cc}; \Cref{sss:cor:not-topos} shows it is not a topos.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->

        \cite{Dub79} and, for the version with additional structure, \cite{MMS22}. The explicit

        closedness and the classifier, are given in \Cref{sss:sec:constructions,sss:sec:cc}; \Cref{sss:cor:not-topos} shows it is not a topos.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{sss:lem:initial-final}
    Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a set.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For any family of maps $f_j:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}_j$ into sample-smooth spaces, the families
            $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} := \left \{  p \,\middle|\, \forall j.\ f_j\circ p \in \mathcal{Y}_j^{\Omega_n}\right \} $ form a sample-smooth
            structure, the \emph{initial} one: it is the largest for which all $f_j$ are
            sample-smooth, and a map $g:\,\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{X}$ is sample-smooth iff every $f_j\circ g$ is.
        \item For any family of maps $e_j:\,\mathcal{W}_j\to\mathcal{X}$ out of sample-smooth spaces, the
            families $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} := \left \{  \text{constants}\right \}  \cup \bigcup_j e_j\circ\mathcal{W}_j^{\Omega_n}$ form a
            sample-smooth structure, the \emph{final} one: it is the smallest for which all $e_j$ are
            sample-smooth, and $g:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}$ is sample-smooth iff every $g\circ e_j$ is.
    \end{enumerate}
    In particular $\mathbf{SSS}$ is topological over $\mathbf{Sets}$, hence complete and cocomplete, with limits and
    colimits computed on underlying sets and equipped with the initial resp.\ final structure.
    \begin{proof}
        Both families contain the constants and are closed under precomposition by (P2) for the
        $\mathcal{Y}_j$ resp.\ $\mathcal{W}_j$; the universal properties are immediate from the definitions.
        Existence of initial structures for arbitrary sources is the definition of a topological
        category over $\mathbf{Sets}$, and such categories are complete and cocomplete with limits and
        colimits lifted from $\mathbf{Sets}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Both families contain the constants and are closed under precomposition by (P2) for the
        $\mathcal{Y}_j$ resp.\ $\mathcal{W}_j$; the universal properties are immediate from the definitions.
        Existence of initial structures for arbitrary sources is the definition of a topological
        category over $\mathbf{Sets}$, and such categories are complete and cocomplete with limits and
        colimits lifted from $\mathbf{Sets}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- prp-6: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:prod-coprod}
    Let $\left ( \mathcal{X}_i\right ) _{i \in I}$ be sample-smooth spaces. Then
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \textstyle\prod_i\mathcal{X}_i\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &= \textstyle\prod_i \mathcal{X}_i^{\Omega_n}, &
        \left ( \textstyle\coprod_i\mathcal{X}_i\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &= \textstyle\bigcup_i \iota_i \circ \mathcal{X}_i^{\Omega_n},
    \end{align}
    the product taken on underlying sets. In particular a plot of a coproduct takes its values in a
    single summand, so $\mathbf{1} \sqcup \mathbf{1} = \breve{\mathbf{2}}$ and not ${\text{\b{$\mathbf{2}$}}}$: coproducts are \emph{rigid}.
    \begin{proof}
        The product carries the initial structure for the projections, which is the displayed
        family; the coproduct carries the final structure for the injections, which is the displayed
        family since the constants are already contained in it (for $I \ne \emptyset$).
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The product carries the initial structure for the projections, which is the displayed
        family; the coproduct carries the final structure for the injections, which is the displayed
        family since the constants are already contained in it (for $I \ne \emptyset$).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
\label{sss:rem:no-jump}
    \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod} says more than the corresponding statement for curves alone, namely
    that a smooth curve into a coproduct stays in one summand, which is a connectedness fact about
    $\mathbb{R}$. Here it also says that a \emph{random} plot cannot jump: a map
    $\Omega_n\to\mathcal{X}_1\sqcup\mathcal{X}_2$ that is a plot must land in one summand for all
    $(t,\omega)$ at once, not merely for each $\omega$ separately. This is the rigidity of
    \cite{For21} on the $\Omega$-side and of connectedness on the $\mathbb{R}$-side, in one statement, and
    it is why we do not impose patching, \Cref{site:rem:no-locality}(3).
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- def-9: body_md -->
\label{sss:def:emb-quot}
    A sample-smooth $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is an \emph{embedding} if it is injective and $\mathcal{X}$ carries
    the initial structure, $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} = \left \{  p \,\middle|\, f \circ p \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}\right \} $, and a \emph{quotient}
    if it is surjective and $\mathcal{Y}$ carries the final structure,
    $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n} = \left \{ \text{constants}\right \} \cup f\circ\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$.
<!-- end def-9 -->
<!-- prp-7: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:eq-coeq}
    Let $f,g:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ be sample-smooth. The equalizer of $(f,g)$ is the set
    $\left \{  x \,\middle|\, f(x) = g(x)\right \} $ with the subspace structure of \Cref{sss:def:emb-quot}, and the
    coequalizer is the set-theoretic coequalizer with the final structure. Monomorphisms are exactly
    the injective sample-smooth maps and epimorphisms exactly the surjective ones; the strong
    monomorphisms are exactly the embeddings and the strong epimorphisms exactly the quotients.
    \begin{proof}
        The first two are \Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}. A sample-smooth map is monic iff it is
        injective, because $\mathbf{1}$ is a generator: two maps $\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{X}$ agreeing after $f$ agree
        pointwise. It is epic iff it is surjective, because ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ is a cogenerator: every map of
        underlying sets into ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ is sample-smooth, so if $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is not surjective
        then $\mathds{1}_{f(\mathcal{X})}$ and $\mathrm{const}_1$ are distinct morphisms $\mathcal{Y}\to{\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$
        agreeing after $f$; the converse is immediate on underlying maps.

        A strong mono is a mono right-orthogonal to all epis. Let $m:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ be a strong
        mono, write $\mathcal{X}'$ for the underlying set of $\mathcal{X}$ with the initial structure along $m$,
        and note that $\mathrm{id}:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}'$ is sample-smooth --- since
        $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}\subseteq\mathcal{X}'^{\Omega_n}$ --- and epic, being surjective. Orthogonality in
        the square $m\circ\mathrm{id} = m$ produces a sample-smooth lift $\mathcal{X}'\to\mathcal{X}$ over the
        identity, whence $\mathcal{X}'^{\Omega_n}\subseteq\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and $m$ is an embedding.
        Conversely an embedding has the lifting property, because a lift exists on underlying sets
        (the epi being surjective, the mono injective) and is sample-smooth by initiality.

        Dually, a quotient is left-orthogonal to every mono, the lift existing on underlying sets
        and being sample-smooth by finality, so quotients are strong epis; and if $f$ is a strong
        epi then, writing $\mathcal{Y}''$ for the underlying set of $\mathcal{Y}$ with the final structure
        along $f$, the map $\mathrm{id}:\,\mathcal{Y}''\to\mathcal{Y}$ is a mono, and orthogonality in
        $\mathrm{id}\circ f = f$ gives a sample-smooth $\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Y}''$ over the identity, so
        $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}''^{\Omega_n}$ and $f$ is a quotient.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-7 -->

<!-- prp-8: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:classifier}
    Let $\top:\,\mathbf{1}\to{\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ pick out $1$. For every embedding $m:\,\mathcal{X}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ there is a
    unique sample-smooth $\chi_m:\,\mathcal{Y}\to{\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ making
    \begin{align}
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \mathcal{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathbf{1} \\
            \downarrow m & & \downarrow \top \\
            \mathcal{Y} & \stackrel{\chi_m}{\longrightarrow} & {\bar{\mathbf{2}}}
        \end{array}
    \end{align}
    a pullback, namely the indicator of $m(\mathcal{X})$.
    \begin{proof}
        Every map into ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ is sample-smooth, since ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}^{\Omega_n}$ is all maps; so $\chi_m$ is a
        morphism and is unique as a map of sets. The pullback of $\top$ along $\chi_m$ is
        $\chi_m^{-1}(1) = m(\mathcal{X})$ with the initial structure, \Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}(1),
        which is $\mathcal{X}$ precisely because $m$ is an embedding.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Every map into ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}$ is sample-smooth, since ${\bar{\mathbf{2}}}^{\Omega_n}$ is all maps; so $\chi_m$ is a
        morphism and is unique as a map of sets. The pullback of $\top$ along $\chi_m$ is
        $\chi_m^{-1}(1) = m(\mathcal{X})$ with the initial structure, \Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}(1),
        which is $\mathcal{X}$ precisely because $m$ is an embedding.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{sss:cor:not-topos}
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ is not a topos. Indeed the identity of $\left \{ 0,1\right \} $ is a monomorphism
    $\breve{\mathbf{2}} \to {\text{\b{$\mathbf{2}$}}}$ which is not an embedding: the initial structure it induces on the source is
    ${\text{\b{$\mathbf{2}$}}}$, whereas $\breve{\mathbf{2}}^\Omega$ consists of the constants alone, and the two differ.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- def-10: body_md -->
\label{sss:def:function-space}
    For $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ let $\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X} := \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ with
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &:= \Big\{\, F:\,\Omega_n \to \mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X} \ \Big|\
        \forall m\ \forall h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)\ \forall q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}: \nonumber \\
        &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad
        \left (  u \mapsto F(h(u))\left (  q(u)\right ) \right )  \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m} \,\Big\} ,
        \label{eq:function-space}
    \end{align}
    where $u$ ranges over $\Omega_m$.
<!-- end def-10 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{sss:lem:function-space-wd}
    \Cref{eq:function-space} defines a sample-smooth structure. Moreover, if one starts from maps
    $F:\,\Omega_n\to\mathbf{Sets}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ and imposes \Cref{eq:function-space}, then every
    value $F(v)$ is automatically sample-smooth, so no separate hypothesis is needed.
    \begin{proof}
        (P1): for constant $F \equiv f$ with $f$ sample-smooth, $u \mapsto f(q(u))$ lies in
        $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$. (P2): for $h_0 \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_n)$ the condition for $F\circ h_0$
        quantifies over $h_0\circ h$, which ranges inside $\mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$.

        For the last claim fix $v \in \Omega_n$ and take $h$ to be the constant morphism
        $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ at $v$, which lies in $\mathbb{S}$ by \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}. Then
        $u \mapsto F(v)(q(u))$ lies in $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$ for every $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$, i.e.\ $F(v)$ is
        sample-smooth.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
(P1): for constant $F \equiv f$ with $f$ sample-smooth, $u \mapsto f(q(u))$ lies in
        $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$. (P2): for $h_0 \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_k,\Omega_n)$ the condition for $F\circ h_0$
        quantifies over $h_0\circ h$, which ranges inside $\mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$.

        For the last claim fix $v \in \Omega_n$ and take $h$ to be the constant morphism
        $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$ at $v$, which lies in $\mathbb{S}$ by \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}. Then
        $u \mapsto F(v)(q(u))$ lies in $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$ for every $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$, i.e.\ $F(v)$ is
        sample-smooth.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ is cartesian closed: evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:\,\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is sample-smooth
    and for every $\mathcal{Z}$ the map
    \begin{align}
        \mathrm{cur}:\; \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X},\ \mathcal{Y}\right )  &\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathcal{Z},\ \mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\right ) , &
        \mathrm{cur}(f)(z)(x) &= f(z,x),
    \end{align}
    is a bijection, natural in all three variables.
    \begin{proof}
        \emph{Evaluation.} A plot of $\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$ on $\Omega_m$ is a pair $(F,q)$ with
        $F \in (\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_m}$ and $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$, by \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. Taking
        $h := \mathrm{id}_{\Omega_m}$ in \Cref{eq:function-space} gives
        $u\mapsto F(u)(q(u)) \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$, which is $\mathrm{ev}\circ(F,q)$.

        \emph{$\mathrm{cur}$ is well defined.} Let $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ and
        $r \in \mathcal{Z}^{\Omega_n}$. For $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ the pair
        $(r\circ h,\,q)$ is a plot of $\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X}$ on $\Omega_m$, so
        $u\mapsto f\left (  r(h(u)),q(u)\right ) $ lies in $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$; this is \Cref{eq:function-space} for
        $\mathrm{cur}(f)\circ r$, so $\mathrm{cur}(f)$ is sample-smooth.

        \emph{$\mathrm{cur}$ is bijective.} Its inverse is $g \mapsto \mathrm{unc}(g)$, $\mathrm{unc}(g)(z,x) := g(z)(x)$,
        which is sample-smooth by the evaluation step applied to $(g\circ r,q)$. The two
        constructions are mutually inverse on underlying maps.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
\emph{Evaluation.} A plot of $\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$ on $\Omega_m$ is a pair $(F,q)$ with
        $F \in (\mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_m}$ and $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$, by \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. Taking
        $h := \mathrm{id}_{\Omega_m}$ in \Cref{eq:function-space} gives
        $u\mapsto F(u)(q(u)) \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$, which is $\mathrm{ev}\circ(F,q)$.

        \emph{$\mathrm{cur}$ is well defined.} Let $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ and
        $r \in \mathcal{Z}^{\Omega_n}$. For $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and $q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$ the pair
        $(r\circ h,\,q)$ is a plot of $\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X}$ on $\Omega_m$, so
        $u\mapsto f\left (  r(h(u)),q(u)\right ) $ lies in $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$; this is \Cref{eq:function-space} for
        $\mathrm{cur}(f)\circ r$, so $\mathrm{cur}(f)$ is sample-smooth.

        \emph{$\mathrm{cur}$ is bijective.} Its inverse is $g \mapsto \mathrm{unc}(g)$, $\mathrm{unc}(g)(z,x) := g(z)(x)$,
        which is sample-smooth by the evaluation step applied to $(g\circ r,q)$. The two
        constructions are mutually inverse on underlying maps.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- prp-9: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:fibre}
    For sample-smooth $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}$ and $g:\,\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}$ the fibre product
    $\mathcal{X}\times_\mathcal{Z}\mathcal{Y}$ is the set-theoretic one with the subspace structure inherited from
    $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$, i.e.
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \mathcal{X}\times_\mathcal{Z}\mathcal{Y}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &= \left \{  (p,q) \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}\times
        \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n} \,\middle|\, f\circ p = g\circ q \right \}  .
    \end{align}
    \begin{proof}
        \Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}(1) applied to the equalizer of $f\circ\mathrm{pr}_\mathcal{X}$ and
        $g\circ\mathrm{pr}_\mathcal{Y}$ inside $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
\Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}(1) applied to the equalizer of $f\circ\mathrm{pr}_\mathcal{X}$ and
        $g\circ\mathrm{pr}_\mathcal{Y}$ inside $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prp-10: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:internal-hom}
    Let $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}$ and $g:\,\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}$ be sample-smooth, and give each fibre
    $f^{-1}(z)$, $g^{-1}(z)$ its subspace structure. Put
    \begin{align}
        {\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g) &:= \bigsqcup_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \mathbf{SSS}\left (  f^{-1}(z),\ g^{-1}(z)\right ) ,
    \end{align}
    with $\varpi:\,{\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g) \to \mathcal{Z}$ sending the summand at $z$ to $z$, and let
    \begin{align}
        {\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g)^{\Omega_n} &:= \Big\{\, F \ \Big|\ \varpi\circ F \in \mathcal{Z}^{\Omega_n}
        \text{ and, for all } m,\ h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n) \text{ and} \nonumber \\
        &\qquad q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m} \text{ with } f\circ q = \varpi\circ F\circ h, \quad
        \left (  u \mapsto F(h(u))\left (  q(u)\right ) \right )  \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m} \,\Big\} .
        \label{eq:internal-hom}
    \end{align}
    Then ${\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g)$ is the exponential $g^f$ in the slice category $\mathbf{SSS}_{/\mathcal{Z}}$. In
    particular $\mathbf{SSS}$ is locally cartesian closed.
    \begin{proof}
        \Cref{eq:internal-hom} is a sample-smooth structure, and the adjunction
        \begin{align}
            \mathbf{SSS}_{/\mathcal{Z}}\left (  e \times_\mathcal{Z} f,\ g\right )  &\cong
            \mathbf{SSS}_{/\mathcal{Z}}\left (  e,\ {\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g)\right ) 
        \end{align}
        is verified exactly as in \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}, every step read over $\mathcal{Z}$
        and the fibre products computed by \Cref{sss:prp:fibre}; for $\mathcal{Z} = \mathbf{1}$ it \emph{is}
        \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}. Local cartesian closedness is also part of
        \Cref{sss:thm:quasitopos}, and we record the formula because it is what one computes with.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->

            \mathbf{SSS}_{/\mathcal{Z}}\left (  e,\ {\mathcal{SSS}}_\mathcal{Z}(f,g)\right ) 
        \end{align}
        is verified exactly as in \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}, every step read over $\mathcal{Z}$

        \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}. Local cartesian closedness is also part of
        \Cref{sss:thm:quasitopos}, and we record the formula because it is what one computes with.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{sss:thm:euclidean}
    $\mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^l\right )  = C^\infty\left ( \mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^l\right ) $, and more generally
    $\left ( \mathbb{R}^l\right ) ^{\mathbb{R}^k} = C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^k,\mathbb{R}^l)$.
    \begin{proof}
        A $C^\infty$ map $f$ preserves plots: if $p \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^k\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ then $f\circ p$ satisfies (M1) by
        the chain rule and (M2) because $f$ is Borel. Conversely let $f$ be sample-smooth. The map
        $\mathrm{pr}:\,(t,\omega)\mapsto t$ lies in $\left ( \mathbb{R}^k\right ) ^{\Omega_k}$, so $f\circ\mathrm{pr} \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^l\right ) ^{\Omega_k}$,
        which by (M1) says that $t \mapsto f(t)$ is $C^\infty$. The second claim is the same
        argument.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
A $C^\infty$ map $f$ preserves plots: if $p \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^k\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ then $f\circ p$ satisfies (M1) by
        the chain rule and (M2) because $f$ is Borel. Conversely let $f$ be sample-smooth. The map
        $\mathrm{pr}:\,(t,\omega)\mapsto t$ lies in $\left ( \mathbb{R}^k\right ) ^{\Omega_k}$, so $f\circ\mathrm{pr} \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^l\right ) ^{\Omega_k}$,
        which by (M1) says that $t \mapsto f(t)$ is $C^\infty$. The second claim is the same
        argument.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
\label{sss:rem:no-boman}
    In a theory whose smooth test object is the line, \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean} is exactly Boman's
    theorem \cite{Bom67}: a map $\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^l$ taking smooth curves to smooth curves is $C^\infty$.
    Here it is immediate, because the site contains $\Omega_k$ and hence the plot $(t,\omega)\mapsto
    t$, which is the identity of $\mathbb{R}^k$ in disguise. The same remark applies to
    \Cref{sss:thm:manifolds}. This is a genuine simplification of the foundations, and it is bought
    with the loss recorded in \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}.
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{sss:thm:manifolds}
    With the structure of \Cref{sss:eg:manifolds}, the assignment $M \mapsto M$ is a full and
    faithful functor from the category of finite-dimensional second-countable Hausdorff smooth
    manifolds and smooth maps into $\mathbf{SSS}$, and it preserves finite products.
    \begin{proof}
        Faithfulness is clear, morphisms being maps of underlying sets. If $f:\,M\to N$ is smooth
        then it preserves plots, by the chain rule and by Borel measurability of $f$. Conversely
        let $f$ be sample-smooth and let $x \in M$. Choose a chart around $x$ whose image is an open
        ball and compose with a diffeomorphism $\mathbb{R}^m \stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}$ ball, giving
        $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,M)$ open onto its image with $x$ in that image. Then
        $(t,\omega)\mapsto\varphi(t)$ lies in $M^{\Omega_m}$, so $f\circ\varphi \in N^{\Omega_m}$, whose (M1$_N$) says
        $f\circ\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,N)$; as $\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open
        neighbourhood of $x$, $f$ is smooth near $x$. Products: the plot family of $M\times N$ in
        the sense of \Cref{sss:eg:manifolds} is the product family of
        \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}, since smoothness and measurability into a product are
        componentwise.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
