<!-- prp-11: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:diffeology}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ let $\mathrm{Dfg}(\mathcal{X})$ be the set $\mathcal{X}$ with, for each $n \ge 0$ and
    each open $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the plots
    \begin{align}
        \mathrm{Dfg}(\mathcal{X})_V &:= \Big\{\, p:\,V\to\mathcal{X} \ \Big|\ \text{every point of } V
        \text{ has a neighbourhood } V' \nonumber \\
        &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \text{on which } p \text{ factors as } \gamma\circ\varphi
        \,\Big\},
    \end{align}
    the factorisation running over $m \ge 0$, $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^m}$ and
    $\varphi \in C^\infty(V',\mathbb{R}^m)$. Then $\mathrm{Dfg}(\mathcal{X})$ is a diffeological space in the
    sense of \cite{Sou80,IZ13}, $\mathrm{Dfg}$ is a functor $\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{Diff}$, and for a manifold $M$
    as in \Cref{sss:eg:manifolds} the diffeology $\mathrm{Dfg}(M)$ is the usual one, consisting of
    all smooth maps $V \to M$.
    \begin{proof}
        Constants factor with $m := 0$. If $\psi \in C^\infty(V'',V)$ and $p$ is a plot then
        $p\circ\psi$ is one, since locally $p\circ\psi = \gamma\circ(\varphi\circ\psi)$. The sheaf
        condition holds because the defining property is local by construction. For functoriality,
        a sample-smooth $f$ sends $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^m}$ into $\mathcal{Y}^{\mathbb{R}^m}$, so it sends a local
        factorisation $\gamma\circ\varphi$ to $(f\circ\gamma)\circ\varphi$.

        For a manifold, $M^{\mathbb{R}^m} = C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,M)$ by \Cref{sss:thm:manifolds}, so every
        $\mathrm{Dfg}(M)$-plot is locally smooth, hence smooth. Conversely let $p \in C^\infty(V,M)$
        and $x \in V$; choose a ball $V' \ni x$ inside $V$ and a diffeomorphism
        $\varphi:\,V' \stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{R}^n$, and put $\gamma := p|_{V'}\circ\varphi^{-1} \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,M)$.
        Then $p|_{V'} = \gamma\circ\varphi$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-11 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->

        Then $p|_{V'} = \gamma\circ\varphi$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
\label{sss:rem:diffeology}
    \Cref{sss:prp:diffeology} goes one way only, and the reason is the subject of this paper. A
    diffeological space carries no admissible random variables, so producing a sample-smooth space
    from one requires supplying them; and once they are supplied, the mixed plots are \emph{still} a
    further choice, by \Cref{site:rem:mixed}. The supplied data must first be compatible in the
    sense of \Cref{sss:lem:Q4}, that $\gamma\circ W \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ for every global plot
    $\gamma$ of the diffeology and every measurable $W$; without that the two kinds of datum do not
    fit together at all, since (P2) applied to $\left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle $ forces $\gamma\circ W$ into the
    random variables. Given compatibility, the generated structure --- the smallest plot family
    containing $\left \{ \gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m}\right \}  \cup \left \{  X\circ\pi_n\right \} $, for $\gamma$ a global
    plot and $X$ a supplied random variable, and closed under $\mathbb{S}$ --- is the smallest choice and
    \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} the largest; whether the two ends of that interval can differ is
    \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}. Note also that $\mathrm{Dfg}$ forgets in the
    smooth direction as well, since a diffeology is determined by its plots on all open $V$ whereas
    a sample-smooth space knows only the global ones; that is the locality discussed in
    \Cref{site:rem:no-locality,disc:rem:locality}.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
\label{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}
A sample-smooth space is not \emph{presented} by $\left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega,\mathcal{X}^\mathbb{R}\right ) $: the plot
    families at $\Omega_n$, $n \ge 1$, are separate data rather than something computed from the
    random variables and the curves. What they are constrained by is one inclusion. The largest
    structure with given $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ and $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ is
    \begin{align}
        \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{  p \,\middle|\, p(-,\omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}\ \forall \omega,\ \text{ and }\
        p \circ h \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega\ \forall h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n) \right \}  ,
        \label{eq:maximal-extension}
    \end{align}
    --- that this is the largest such structure is immediate, since by
    \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs} every $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ satisfies both conditions ---
    and $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} \subseteq \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ may in principle be strict. This is the
    price of \Cref{site:rem:mixed}, and it is not a defect to be repaired: it is exactly the room in
    which \Cref{prob:def:PrPf} is made. \Cref{prob:rem:comparison} identifies the question of
    equality in \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} for $\mathcal{X} := \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ as a measurable selection
    problem.

    Three things should be said precisely. First, $\widehat\mathcal{X}$ is itself an object of $\mathbf{SSS}$:
    \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} contains the constants and is closed under precomposition, because
    $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ is closed under precomposition with smooth maps by \Cref{site:prp:karoubi} and
    because $h_0\circ h$ again lies in $\mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$. Second, $\widehat\mathcal{X}$ has the
    same underlying set, the same random variables and the same $n$-parameter families as $\mathcal{X}$
    --- see the proof of \Cref{sss:prp:reflection}(1) --- and the identity is a sample-smooth
    map $\mathcal{X}\to\widehat\mathcal{X}$; so the comparison is between
    two genuine objects, and it is an isomorphism exactly when \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} is an
    equality. Third, and honestly: we know of \emph{no} $\mathcal{X}$ for which the inclusion is strict.
    It is an equality for $\mathbb{R}^k$ and for manifolds, where the first condition of
    \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} is the smoothness condition defining the plots and the second, taken
    at $h := \iota^n_t$, is the measurability condition; for
    $\flat\mathcal{S}$, whose plots are the $t$-independent ones on both sides; and for $\sharp\mathcal{S}$,
    where both sides are defined by the same substitution condition; and it is inherited by
    products, both conditions being componentwise. Whether it can fail at all --- and in particular
    whether it fails at $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$, which is the question of \Cref{prob:rem:comparison} --- we
    do not know. Until that is settled one cannot rule out that every object of $\mathbf{SSS}$ is after all
    recovered from its random variables together with its $n$-parameter families --- which is less
    than being recovered from its \emph{curves}, since we have not shown that $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ is
    determined by $\mathcal{X}^\mathbb{R}$ either.
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- prp-12: body_md -->
\label{sss:prp:reflection}
    The assignment $\mathcal{X} \mapsto \widehat\mathcal{X}$ of \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} extends to a
    functor $\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{SSS}$ which is the identity on underlying sets and on maps, and:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\widehat{\widehat\mathcal{X}} = \widehat\mathcal{X}$, and the identity
            $\eta_\mathcal{X}:\,\mathcal{X}\to\widehat\mathcal{X}$ is a natural transformation
            $\mathrm{id}_\mathbf{SSS}\Rightarrow\widehat{(-)}$;
        \item writing $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ for the full subcategory of the \emph{presented}
            objects, those with $\mathcal{X} = \widehat\mathcal{X}$, the functor $\widehat{(-)}$ is left
            adjoint to the inclusion $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}\subseteq\mathbf{SSS}$; that is,
            $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ is a reflective subcategory and $\widehat{(-)}$ its reflector,
            with $\eta$ the unit;
        \item $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ contains $\mathbb{R}^k$, every manifold, every rigid and every loose
            object, and is closed under products.
    \end{enumerate}
    An object lies in $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ exactly when its mixed plots are determined by its
    random variables together with its $n$-parameter families, so $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ is the
    category a presentation by those two towers would give --- which is less than a presentation by
    curves, as the last sentence of \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice} notes; and
    \Cref{prob:rem:comparison} is the question whether $\mathsf{P}$ lands in it.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$. Then $f$ carries $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ into $\mathcal{Y}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$,
        since $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ gives
        $f\circ\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$, and it carries $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$
        into $\mathcal{Y}^\Omega$. So for $p \in \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ both defining conditions
        of \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} pass to $f\circ p$, and
        $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\widehat\mathcal{X},\widehat\mathcal{Y})$: the assignment is functorial. It is the
        identity on underlying sets by construction, so naturality of $\eta$ is the commuting of a
        square of identities, and $\eta_\mathcal{X}$ is sample-smooth because
        $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} \subseteq \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$.

        (1) $\widehat\mathcal{X}$ has the same random variables and the same $n$-parameter families as
        $\mathcal{X}$. For the first, take $h := \mathrm{id}_\Omega \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_0)$ in the
        second condition of \Cref{eq:maximal-extension}, giving
        $\widehat\mathcal{X}^\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{X}^\Omega$, the reverse inclusion being
        $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}\subseteq\widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ at $n=0$. For the second, if
        $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} \in \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ then the first condition at any
        $\omega$ gives $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$; again the reverse inclusion is immediate. Since
        \Cref{eq:maximal-extension} depends on $\mathcal{X}$ only through those two,
        $\widehat{\widehat\mathcal{X}} = \widehat\mathcal{X}$.

        (2) Let $\mathcal{Y} = \widehat\mathcal{Y}$ and let $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$; we must show that
        the same map of sets lies in $\mathbf{SSS}(\widehat\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$, and uniqueness is then
        automatic, $\eta_\mathcal{X}$ being the identity on underlying sets. Let
        $p \in \widehat\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. For each $\omega$ we have
        $p(-,\omega) \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$, hence $f\circ p(-,\omega) \in \mathcal{Y}^{\mathbb{R}^n}$; and for
        each $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$ we have $p\circ h \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$, hence
        $f\circ p\circ h \in \mathcal{Y}^\Omega$. So $f\circ p \in \widehat\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n} =
        \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$.

        (3) is the list of equalities established in
        \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-12 -->

<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
\label{sss:rem:reflection}
    Three things. It names the comparison: the whole difference between the present category and one
    presented by $n$-parameter families and random variables is the difference between $\mathbf{SSS}$ and
    $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$, and \Cref{prob:rem:comparison} asks whether that difference is visible
    at $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ --- indeed whether it is visible anywhere. It sorts out the two fallbacks
    alluded to in \Cref{disc:sec:related}: on $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ one has the endofunctor
    $\widehat{\mathsf{P}(-)}$, whose multiplication has no reason to survive the reflection, and one has
    $\mathsf{P}$ itself read as a functor $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}\to\mathbf{SSS}$, which is a monad
    \emph{relative} to the inclusion \cite{ACU15,Man76} --- automatically so, the inclusion being
    fully faithful and $\mathsf{P}$ a monad on $\mathbf{SSS}$. And it locates the cost: $\mathbf{SSS}_{\mathrm{pr}}$, being
    reflective, inherits limits from $\mathbf{SSS}$ but computes colimits by reflecting them, so the two
    categories agree on everything in \Cref{sec:sss} that is built from limits and differ at most
    on quotients --- of which \Cref{prob:def:PrPf} is one.
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- def-11: body_md -->
\label{tan:def:tangent}
    Let $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ and let $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbf{SSS}(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{X})$ be the function space of
    \Cref{sss:def:function-space}, whose underlying set is the set of admissible curves. Define an
    equivalence relation on it by
    \begin{align}
        \gamma \sim \eta \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma(0) = \eta(0) \ \text{ and }\
        \left (  f\circ\gamma\right ) '(0) = \left (  f\circ\eta\right ) '(0) \ \text{ for all } f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R}),
        \label{eq:tangent-equiv}
    \end{align}
    which makes sense because $f\circ\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}} = C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ by
    \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean}. Put $T\mathcal{X} := \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}/\!\sim$ with the quotient structure of
    \Cref{sss:def:emb-quot}, write $[\gamma]$ for the class of $\gamma$, and let
    $\pi_\mathcal{X}:\,T\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}$, $[\gamma]\mapsto\gamma(0)$. The \emph{tangent space at $x$} is the
    subobject $T_x\mathcal{X} := \pi_\mathcal{X}^{-1}(x)$.
<!-- end def-11 -->
<!-- prp-13: body_md -->
\label{tan:prp:functor}
    $\pi_\mathcal{X}$ is sample-smooth. For sample-smooth $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ the assignment
    $Tf[\gamma] := [f\circ\gamma]$ is well defined and sample-smooth, $T$ is an endofunctor of
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ with $\pi$ natural, and
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{R}\times T\mathcal{X} &\longrightarrow T\mathcal{X}, &
        \left ( \lambda,[\gamma]\right )  &\longmapsto \lambda\cdot[\gamma] := \left [  t\mapsto\gamma(\lambda t)\right ] ,
    \end{align}
    is sample-smooth and restricts to a scalar action on each $T_x\mathcal{X}$ fixing
    $[\mathrm{const}_x]$. We write $df_x := T_xf:\,T_x\mathcal{X}\to T_{f(x)}\mathcal{Y}$ for the
    \emph{differential} of $f$ at $x$; the transpose $df^*_x$ on cotangent vectors is
    \Cref{tan:prp:cotangent} below.
    \begin{proof}
        $\pi_\mathcal{X}$ composed with the quotient map is $\mathrm{ev}_0$, which is sample-smooth by
        \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}, so $\pi_\mathcal{X}$ is sample-smooth by finality,
        \Cref{sss:lem:initial-final}(2). If $\gamma\sim\eta$ then, for $g \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{Y},\mathbb{R})$, we
        have $g\circ f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R})$, so $(g\circ f\circ\gamma)'(0) = (g\circ f\circ\eta)'(0)$;
        together with $f(\gamma(0)) = f(\eta(0))$ this gives $f\circ\gamma\sim f\circ\eta$, so $Tf$
        is well defined, and it is sample-smooth by
        finality because $\gamma\mapsto f\circ\gamma$ is sample-smooth
        $\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathcal{Y}^{\mathbb{R}}$. Functoriality is immediate. For the scalar action,
        $(\lambda,\gamma)\mapsto\gamma(\lambda\,\cdot)$ is sample-smooth
        $\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}$ by \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}, it respects
        $\sim$ because $\left (  f\circ\gamma(\lambda\,\cdot)\right ) '(0) = \lambda\,(f\circ\gamma)'(0)$, and
        $\mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}\times q$ is again a quotient map: writing $q$ for the quotient map of
        \Cref{tan:def:tangent}, one has $\left (  T\mathcal{X}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} = q\circ\left ( \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}
        \right ) ^{\Omega_n}$, the constants being images of constant plots, whence
        $\left ( \mathbb{R}\times T\mathcal{X}\right ) ^{\Omega_n} = \left ( \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}\times q\right ) \circ\left ( \mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}
        \right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ by \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. So the map descends and is sample-smooth by
        finality.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-13 -->

<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{tan:thm:euclidean}
    The map $\gamma\mapsto\left ( \gamma(0),\gamma'(0)\right ) $ induces an isomorphism
    \begin{align}
        T\mathbb{R}^n &\;\cong\; \mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n,
    \end{align}
    under which $T_x\mathbb{R}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ for every $x$, and for $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n) =
    C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^n)$ the map $Tf$ becomes
    \begin{align}
        Tf(x,v) &= \left (  f(x),\ Df(x)\,v\right )  ,
    \end{align}
    with $Df$ the Jacobian. In particular $Df:\,\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ is sample-smooth, and all
    higher derivatives are obtained by iterating $T$.
    \begin{proof}
        Write $\beta(\gamma) := \left ( \gamma(0),\gamma'(0)\right ) $. Since $\mathbf{SSS}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}) = C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R})$
        by \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean}, the relation \Cref{eq:tangent-equiv} holds precisely when
        $\beta(\gamma) = \beta(\eta)$: ``$\Leftarrow$'' is the chain rule, and ``$\Rightarrow$''
        follows by taking for $f$ the $n$ coordinate projections.

        $\beta$ is sample-smooth: a plot of $\left ( \mathbb{R}^n\right ) ^{\mathbb{R}}$ on $\Omega_m$ is an $F$ for which
        $G(s,\omega,t) := F(s,\omega)(t)$ is smooth in $(s,t)$ jointly and measurable in $\omega$,
        by \Cref{eq:function-space}; then $G(-,-,0)$ and $\partial_t G(-,-,0)$ are smooth in $s$ and
        measurable in $\omega$, the latter as a pointwise limit of difference quotients.

        Finally $\beta$ is a quotient map, because a plot $(a,b)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$ on $\Omega_m$
        lifts to the plot $u \mapsto \left (  t\mapsto a(u) + t\,b(u)\right ) $. Hence the induced bijection
        $T\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$ is an isomorphism, both sides carrying the final structure for
        $\beta$. The formula for $Tf$ is the chain rule, and sample-smoothness of $Df$
        follows by \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean} from smoothness of $(x,v)\mapsto Df(x)v$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-8 -->

<!-- prp-14: body_md -->
\label{tan:prp:manifolds}
    For a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $M$ as in \Cref{sss:eg:manifolds}, $T M$ is the
    classical tangent bundle, $\pi_M$ is the classical projection, and $Tf$ is the classical
    differential for every smooth $f$.
    \begin{proof}
        Write $T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$ for the classical tangent bundle, itself a manifold and so an
        object by \Cref{sss:eg:manifolds}, and put $\beta_M(\gamma) := \gamma'(0) \in
        T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$, whose base point is $\gamma(0)$.

        The fibres of $\beta_M$ are the $\sim$-classes: ``$\Leftarrow$'' is the chain rule, and
        ``$\Rightarrow$'' holds because $\mathbf{SSS}(M,\mathbb{R}) = C^\infty(M,\mathbb{R})$ by \Cref{sss:thm:manifolds},
        because $(f\circ\gamma)'(0) = df_{\gamma(0)}\left ( \gamma'(0)\right ) $, and because smooth real
        functions separate classical tangent vectors.

        $\beta_M$ is sample-smooth. Smoothness in the parameter is local and may be read in a chart;
        measurability in the seed may not, since the chart around $G(s,\omega,0)$ depends on
        $\omega$, so we argue globally. Let $G \in M^{\mathbb{R}}{}^{\Omega_m}$ be a plot, i.e.\ a map
        $G:\,\mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\to M$ smooth in $(s,t)$ and admissible in $\omega$, and
        fix $s$. Cover $M$ by countably many chart domains $U_i$ with charts $\kappa_i$, which is
        possible because $M$ is second-countable, and put
        \begin{align}
            E_{i,k} &:= \bigcap_{t \in \mathbb{Q},\ |t|\le 1/k}
            \left \{  \omega \,\middle|\, G(s,\omega,t) \in U_i \right \}  ,
        \end{align}
        which lies in $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ by (M2$_M$) for $G$. The $E_{i,k}$ cover $\Omega$, since each
        curve $G(s,\omega,-)$ is continuous at $0$. On
        $E_{i,k}$ the classical derivative $\partial_tG(s,\omega,0)$ is the pointwise limit as
        $j\to\infty$ of $j\left ( \kappa_i G(s,\omega,1/j) - \kappa_i G(s,\omega,0)\right ) $, $j\ge k$,
        each term measurable in $\omega$; so $\omega\mapsto\beta_M(G(s,\omega,-))$ is measurable
        on each $E_{i,k}$, hence on $\Omega$.

        $\beta_M$ is a quotient map. Here a \emph{global} lift is needed, since
        \Cref{site:rem:no-locality} leaves no way to subdivide the domain of a plot and reglue.
        Equip $M$ with a complete Riemannian metric, which exists because $M$ is second-countable
        and Hausdorff, so that $\exp:\,T^{\mathrm{cl}}M \to M$ is defined on all of
        $T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$ and smooth. Given a plot $w:\,\Omega_m\to T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$ put
        \begin{align}
            F(u) &:= \left (  t \mapsto \exp\left (  t \cdot w(u)\right ) \right ) , \qquad u \in \Omega_m,
        \end{align}
        with $t\cdot w(u)$ the fibrewise scalar multiple. Then $F$ is a plot of $M^{\mathbb{R}}$, being
        smooth in the two smooth arguments jointly and measurable in the seed, and
        $\beta_M\left (  F(u)\right )  = w(u)$ because
        $\tfrac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\exp(t v) = v$. Hence $T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$ carries the final
        structure for $\beta_M$ and the induced bijection $TM \to T^{\mathrm{cl}}M$ is an
        isomorphism. The statements about $\pi_M$ and $Tf$ follow.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-14 -->

<!-- def-12: body_md -->
\label{tan:def:cotangent}
    For $x \in \mathcal{X}$ let $f \sim_x g$ if $\left (  f\circ\gamma\right ) '(0) = \left (  g\circ\gamma\right ) '(0)$ for
    every $\gamma \in \mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, and put
    $T^*_x\mathcal{X} := \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R})/\!\sim_x$.
<!-- end def-12 -->
<!-- prp-15: body_md -->
\label{tan:prp:cotangent}
    $T^*_x\mathcal{X}$ is a real vector space, and
    \begin{align}
        \left\langle -,-\right\rangle:\; T_x\mathcal{X} \times T^*_x\mathcal{X} &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, &
        \left\langle [\gamma],[f]\right\rangle &:= \left (  f\circ\gamma\right ) '(0),
    \end{align}
    is well defined, separates points in each variable and is homogeneous in the first. For a
    sample-smooth $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ the transpose
    $df^*_x:\,T^*_{f(x)}\mathcal{Y}\to T^*_x\mathcal{X}$, $df^*_x[g] := [g\circ f]$, is well defined and
    linear, and $\left\langle df_x(v),[g]\right\rangle = \left\langle v,df^*_x[g]\right\rangle$ for $df_x$ of
    \Cref{tan:prp:functor}. The pairing is not in general bilinear, because $T_x\mathcal{X}$ need not
    carry a linear structure making it so: for $\mathcal{X} := \left \{  xy=0\right \}  \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ the injection
    $d\iota_0:\,T_0\mathcal{X}\hookrightarrow T_0\mathbb{R}^2 \cong \mathbb{R}^2$ has as image the union of the two axes, which
    is stable under scalars but is not a linear subspace.
    \begin{proof}
        $f\mapsto \left (  \gamma\mapsto (f\circ\gamma)'(0)\right ) $ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear into the vector space of
        functions on the curves through $x$, and $\sim_x$ is the congruence of its kernel, so the
        quotient is a vector space and the pairing is well defined and separating in the second
        variable; it is separating in the first by \Cref{eq:tangent-equiv}. Homogeneity is
        \Cref{tan:prp:functor}. For the transpose, if $g\sim_{f(x)}\tilde g$ then for every
        $\gamma\in\mathcal{X}^\mathbb{R}$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ the curve $f\circ\gamma$ lies in $\mathcal{Y}^\mathbb{R}$ with
        $(f\circ\gamma)(0)=f(x)$, so
        $(g\circ f\circ\gamma)'(0) = (\tilde g\circ f\circ\gamma)'(0)$,
        i.e.\ $g\circ f\sim_x \tilde g\circ f$; linearity and the adjunction identity are then immediate
        from the definitions.

        For the last claim take $\mathcal{X} := \left \{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \,\middle|\, xy = 0\right \} $ with the subspace
        structure. A tangent vector at the origin is determined by the pair
        $\left ( \gamma_1'(0),\gamma_2'(0)\right ) $: let $f \in \mathbf{SSS}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{R})$ and put $h(s) := f(s,0)$,
        $k(s) := f(0,s)$, which lie in $C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ because the two axis inclusions are
        sample-smooth; since at every $t$ at least one coordinate of $\gamma(t)$ vanishes,
        \begin{align}
            f\left ( \gamma(t)\right )  &= h\left ( \gamma_1(t)\right )  + k\left ( \gamma_2(t)\right )  - f(0,0),
        \end{align}
        so $\left (  f\circ\gamma\right ) '(0) = h'(0)\,\gamma_1'(0) + k'(0)\,\gamma_2'(0)$ depends on $\gamma$
        only through that pair. Both $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ occur, from the two axis curves. The pair
        $(1,1)$ does not: if $\gamma_1'(0)\ne0\ne\gamma_2'(0)$ then each $\gamma_i$ is non-zero on a
        punctured neighbourhood of $0$, contradicting $\gamma_1\gamma_2 \equiv 0$. So the image of
        $T_0\mathcal{X}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the union of the two axes, as claimed.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-15 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->

<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
\label{tan:rem:flat}
    A rigid object has no non-constant curves, so $T\flat\mathcal{S} \cong \flat\mathcal{S}$ and every tangent
    space is a point: on the image of $\flat$ the tangent functor is the identity. This is the
    expected reading --- data typed by $\flat$ is data one may not differentiate --- and it is also
    a warning, since it says that $T$ carries no information there. What $T\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ looks like
    we do not know; see \Cref{disc:sec:open}.
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{modal:lem:functors}
    $\natural:\,\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{QUS}$, $\flat:\,\mathbf{QUS}\to\mathbf{SSS}$ and $\sharp:\,\mathbf{QUS}\to\mathbf{SSS}$ of
    \Cref{sss:not:derived,sss:eg:flat-sharp} are functors, and
    $\natural\flat = \natural\sharp = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{QUS}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        Functoriality is immediate in each case. $\left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right ) ^\Omega = \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because
        $\pi_0 = \mathrm{id}_{\Omega_0}$; and $\left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^\Omega = \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because $\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_0}$ is one
        of the $h$ quantified over, giving ``$\subseteq$'', while ``$\supseteq$'' is closure of $\mathcal{S}^\Omega$
        under $\Omega^\Omega$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Functoriality is immediate in each case. $\left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right ) ^\Omega = \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because
        $\pi_0 = \mathrm{id}_{\Omega_0}$; and $\left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^\Omega = \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because $\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_0}$ is one
        of the $h$ quantified over, giving ``$\subseteq$'', while ``$\supseteq$'' is closure of $\mathcal{S}^\Omega$
        under $\Omega^\Omega$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{modal:thm:triple}
    $\flat \dashv \natural \dashv \sharp$, and $\flat$ and $\sharp$ are full and faithful. Consequently
    $\natural$ preserves all limits and colimits, $\flat$ preserves colimits and $\sharp$ preserves
    limits, and $\mathbf{QUS}$ is a full subcategory of $\mathbf{SSS}$ in two ways.
    \begin{proof}
        \emph{$\flat\dashv\natural$.} Let $f:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ be a map. If $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\mathcal{S},\natural\mathcal{X})$
        then for $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ we get $f\circ X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ and hence
        $f\circ (X\circ\pi_n) = (f\circ X)\circ\pi_n \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ by (P2); as the plots of
        $\flat\mathcal{S}$ are exactly the $X\circ\pi_n$, $f$ is sample-smooth. Conversely, taking $n=0$
        and $\pi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ recovers $f\circ X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$.

        \emph{$\natural\dashv\sharp$.} Let $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}$ be a map. It is sample-smooth into
        $\sharp\mathcal{S}$ iff $f\circ p \circ h \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ for every $n$, every
        $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and every $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$. Since $p\circ h \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$
        this is implied by $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\natural\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$, and taking $n=0$, $h=\mathrm{id}$ gives the
        converse.

        Full faithfulness of $\flat$ and $\sharp$ follows from $\natural\flat = \natural\sharp = \mathrm{id}$,
        \Cref{modal:lem:functors}, together with the two adjunctions.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
\emph{$\flat\dashv\natural$.} Let $f:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ be a map. If $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\mathcal{S},\natural\mathcal{X})$
        then for $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ we get $f\circ X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ and hence
        $f\circ (X\circ\pi_n) = (f\circ X)\circ\pi_n \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ by (P2); as the plots of
        $\flat\mathcal{S}$ are exactly the $X\circ\pi_n$, $f$ is sample-smooth. Conversely, taking $n=0$
        and $\pi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ recovers $f\circ X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$.

        \emph{$\natural\dashv\sharp$.} Let $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}$ be a map. It is sample-smooth into
        $\sharp\mathcal{S}$ iff $f\circ p \circ h \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ for every $n$, every
        $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and every $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$. Since $p\circ h \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$
        this is implied by $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\natural\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$, and taking $n=0$, $h=\mathrm{id}$ gives the
        converse.

        Full faithfulness of $\flat$ and $\sharp$ follows from $\natural\flat = \natural\sharp = \mathrm{id}$,
        \Cref{modal:lem:functors}, together with the two adjunctions.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- rem-11: body_md -->
\label{modal:rem:reading}
    $\flat\mathcal{S}$ is $\mathcal{S}$ with \emph{no} differentiable structure: its only $n$-parameter families
    are the constant ones, so a sample-smooth map out of a connected smooth object into $\flat\mathcal{S}$
    is constant. $\sharp\mathcal{S}$ is $\mathcal{S}$ with \emph{no} smoothness requirement: a map into
    $\sharp\mathcal{S}$ is sample-smooth as soon as it is quasi-measurable. In the intended reading of
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ as a semantics, $\flat$ marks data that must not be differentiated and $\sharp$ marks data
    whose differentiable structure is not being tracked.
<!-- end rem-11 -->
<!-- def-13: body_md -->
\label{modal:def:shape}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\mathcal{X}$ generated by
    \begin{align}
        p(t,\omega) &\sim p(t',\omega), \qquad p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_1},\ t,t' \in \mathbb{R},\ \omega \in \Omega .
    \end{align}
    Let $\Pi\mathcal{X} := \mathcal{X}/\!\sim$ with the final quasi-universal structure along the projection
    $q_\mathcal{X}:\,\natural\mathcal{X} \to \Pi\mathcal{X}$, i.e.\
    $\left ( \Pi\mathcal{X}\right ) ^\Omega = q_\mathcal{X} \circ \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ when $\mathcal{X} \ne \mathbf{0}$.
<!-- end def-13 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{modal:lem:shape-arities}
    For $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, $t,t' \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\omega \in \Omega$ one has
    $p(t,\omega)\sim p(t',\omega)$.
    \begin{proof}
        Pick $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $\varphi(0)=t$, $\varphi(1)=t'$, for instance an
        affine path. Then $p \circ \varphi^{(n)} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_1}$ by \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, and it
        joins the two points at the same $\omega$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Pick $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $\varphi(0)=t$, $\varphi(1)=t'$, for instance an
        affine path. Then $p \circ \varphi^{(n)} \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_1}$ by \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, and it
        joins the two points at the same $\omega$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{modal:thm:shape-adjoint}
    $\Pi:\,\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{QUS}$ is a functor and $\Pi \dashv \flat$; moreover $\Pi\flat \cong \mathrm{id}_\mathbf{QUS}$.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}$ be a map. Then $f$ is sample-smooth as a map $\mathcal{X}\to\flat\mathcal{S}$ iff
        for every $n$ and $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ the composite $f\circ p$ is of the form $X\circ\pi_n$
        with $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$; that is, iff (a) $f\circ p$ does not depend on the $\mathbb{R}^n$
        coordinate, and (b) $f\circ p\circ\iota^n_{t_0} \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ for some, hence by (a) for
        every, $t_0$.

        By \Cref{modal:lem:shape-arities}, (a) for all $n,p$ holds iff $f$ is constant on
        $\sim$-classes, i.e.\ iff $f = \bar f \circ q_\mathcal{X}$ for a unique $\bar f$. Given (a),
        condition (b) ranges over exactly the elements $p\circ\iota^n_{t_0}$ of $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$, and
        every element of $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ occurs, so (b) says $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\natural\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$, which by
        finality of $\Pi\mathcal{X}$ says $\bar f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\Pi\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$. The correspondence
        $f \leftrightarrow \bar f$ is the required natural bijection. Finally $\flat\mathcal{S}$ has only
        $t$-independent plots, so $\sim$ is trivial on it and
        $\Pi\flat\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{S}$ with $q = \mathrm{id}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}$ be a map. Then $f$ is sample-smooth as a map $\mathcal{X}\to\flat\mathcal{S}$ iff
        for every $n$ and $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ the composite $f\circ p$ is of the form $X\circ\pi_n$

        every, $t_0$.

        By \Cref{modal:lem:shape-arities}, (a) for all $n,p$ holds iff $f$ is constant on
        $\sim$-classes, i.e.\ iff $f = \bar f \circ q_\mathcal{X}$ for a unique $\bar f$. Given (a),
        condition (b) ranges over exactly the elements $p\circ\iota^n_{t_0}$ of $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$, and
        every element of $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ occurs, so (b) says $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\natural\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$, which by
        finality of $\Pi\mathcal{X}$ says $\bar f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\Pi\mathcal{X},\mathcal{S})$. The correspondence
        $f \leftrightarrow \bar f$ is the required natural bijection. Finally $\flat\mathcal{S}$ has only

        $\Pi\flat\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{S}$ with $q = \mathrm{id}$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- prp-16: body_md -->
\label{modal:prp:shape-products}
    $\Pi\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ and the canonical map
    $\Pi(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}) \to \Pi\mathcal{X}\times\Pi\mathcal{Y}$ is an isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces.
    \begin{proof}
        The map is surjective because $(x,y)$ maps to $([x],[y])$. For injectivity, suppose
        $x \sim x'$ in $\mathcal{X}$ and $y \sim y'$ in $\mathcal{Y}$. It suffices to treat a single generating
        step in each factor. If $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_1}$ joins $x$ to $x'$ at $\omega$, then
        $\left (  p,\mathrm{const}_y\right )  \in (\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{\Omega_1}$ by \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod} joins
        $(x,y)$ to $(x',y)$ at $\omega$; symmetrically for the second factor. Concatenating the two
        chains gives $(x,y)\sim(x',y')$.

        For the structures: $\left ( \Pi\mathcal{X}\times\Pi\mathcal{Y}\right ) ^\Omega =
        \left \{  (q_\mathcal{X}\circ X,\,q_\mathcal{Y}\circ Y) \,\middle|\, X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega,\ Y \in \mathcal{Y}^\Omega\right \} $ by
        \Cref{qus:thm:quasitopos,modal:def:shape}, while
        $\Pi(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^\Omega = \left \{  q\circ(X,Y)\right \} $, and $(X,Y)$ ranges over all pairs by
        \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. The bijection matches the two families.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->

        \Cref{qus:thm:quasitopos,modal:def:shape}, while

        \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. The bijection matches the two families.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{modal:lem:factorisation}
    Let $\mathcal{S} \in \mathbf{QUS}$, $n\ge0$ and $p \in \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$. Then there are $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$
    and $q \in \left ( \sharp\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ with $p = X \circ q$.
    \begin{proof}
        By ($\Omega$5) there is a Borel injection $\iota:\,\mathbb{R}^n\to\Omega$ with Borel image $B$ and
        Borel inverse; let $\rho:\,\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be Borel with $\rho\circ\iota = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, for
        instance $\rho := \iota^{-1}$ on $B$ and $0$ off $B$. Put
        \begin{align}
            q(t,\omega) &:= \Theta^{-1}\left ( \iota(t),\,\omega\right ) , &
            X(\sigma) &:= p\left (  \rho(\Theta_1\sigma),\ \Theta_2\sigma \right )  .
        \end{align}
        Then $X(q(t,\omega)) = p(\rho\iota(t),\omega) = p(t,\omega)$. For
        $q \in \left ( \sharp\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ take $h = \left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle  \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$; then
        $q\circ h = \Theta^{-1}\left ( \iota\circ W,\Phi\right )  \in \Omega^\Omega$ by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}. And $X = p \circ \left \langle \rho\circ\Theta_1,
        \Theta_2\right \rangle $ with $\left \langle \rho\circ\Theta_1,\Theta_2\right \rangle  \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$, so
        $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because $p \in \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By ($\Omega$5) there is a Borel injection $\iota:\,\mathbb{R}^n\to\Omega$ with Borel image $B$ and
        Borel inverse; let $\rho:\,\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be Borel with $\rho\circ\iota = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}^n}$, for
        instance $\rho := \iota^{-1}$ on $B$ and $0$ off $B$. Put
        \begin{align}
            q(t,\omega) &:= \Theta^{-1}\left ( \iota(t),\,\omega\right ) , &
            X(\sigma) &:= p\left (  \rho(\Theta_1\sigma),\ \Theta_2\sigma \right )  .
        \end{align}
        Then $X(q(t,\omega)) = p(\rho\iota(t),\omega) = p(t,\omega)$. For
        $q \in \left ( \sharp\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$ take $h = \left \langle  W,\Phi\right \rangle  \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$; then
        $q\circ h = \Theta^{-1}\left ( \iota\circ W,\Phi\right )  \in \Omega^\Omega$ by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}. And $X = p \circ \left \langle \rho\circ\Theta_1,
        \Theta_2\right \rangle $ with $\left \langle \rho\circ\Theta_1,\Theta_2\right \rangle  \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$, so
        $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ because $p \in \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{modal:thm:lambda}
    Let $\Lambda\mathcal{X} := \left (  \mathcal{X},\ \mathbf{SSS}(\sharp\Omega,\mathcal{X})\right ) $, where a sample-smooth map
    $\sharp\Omega\to\mathcal{X}$ is read as a map $\Omega\to\mathcal{X}$. Then $\Lambda$ is a functor
    $\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{QUS}$ and $\sharp\dashv\Lambda$.
    \begin{proof}
        $\Lambda\mathcal{X}$ is a quasi-universal space: constants are sample-smooth, and for
        $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$ the map $\sharp\Phi:\,\sharp\Omega\to\sharp\Omega$ is sample-smooth
        by \Cref{modal:lem:functors}, so $X\circ\Phi = X\circ\sharp\Phi$ is again sample-smooth.
        Functoriality is postcomposition.

        Let $f:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ be a map. If $f$ is sample-smooth $\sharp\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ then for
        every $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ the composite $f\circ X = f\circ\sharp X$ is sample-smooth
        $\sharp\Omega\to\mathcal{X}$, i.e.\ lies in $(\Lambda\mathcal{X})^\Omega$; so
        $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\mathcal{S},\Lambda\mathcal{X})$. Conversely assume the latter and let
        $p \in \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$. Write $p = X\circ q$ as in \Cref{modal:lem:factorisation}. Then
        $f\circ X \in \mathbf{SSS}(\sharp\Omega,\mathcal{X})$ by hypothesis and $q \in \left ( \sharp\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$, so
        $f\circ p = (f\circ X)\circ q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. Naturality is clear.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
$\Lambda\mathcal{X}$ is a quasi-universal space: constants are sample-smooth, and for
        $\Phi \in \Omega^\Omega$ the map $\sharp\Phi:\,\sharp\Omega\to\sharp\Omega$ is sample-smooth
        by \Cref{modal:lem:functors}, so $X\circ\Phi = X\circ\sharp\Phi$ is again sample-smooth.
        Functoriality is postcomposition.

        Let $f:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ be a map. If $f$ is sample-smooth $\sharp\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{X}$ then for
        every $X \in \mathcal{S}^\Omega$ the composite $f\circ X = f\circ\sharp X$ is sample-smooth
        $\sharp\Omega\to\mathcal{X}$, i.e.\ lies in $(\Lambda\mathcal{X})^\Omega$; so
        $f \in \mathbf{QUS}(\mathcal{S},\Lambda\mathcal{X})$. Conversely assume the latter and let
        $p \in \left ( \sharp\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$. Write $p = X\circ q$ as in \Cref{modal:lem:factorisation}. Then
        $f\circ X \in \mathbf{SSS}(\sharp\Omega,\mathcal{X})$ by hypothesis and $q \in \left ( \sharp\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$, so
        $f\circ p = (f\circ X)\circ q \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. Naturality is clear.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{modal:thm:string}
    There is an adjoint string
    \begin{align}
        \Pi \;\dashv\; \flat \;\dashv\; \natural \;\dashv\; \sharp \;\dashv\; \Lambda,
        \qquad \Pi,\natural,\Lambda:\,\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathbf{QUS}, \quad \flat,\sharp:\,\mathbf{QUS}\to\mathbf{SSS},
    \end{align}
    in which $\flat$ and $\sharp$ are full and faithful and $\Pi$ preserves finite products. In
    particular $\mathbf{SSS}$ is \emph{cohesive} over $\mathbf{QUS}$ in the sense of \cite{Law07}, with the
    additional right adjoint $\Lambda$.
    \begin{proof}
        \Cref{modal:thm:shape-adjoint}, \Cref{modal:thm:triple}, \Cref{modal:thm:lambda,modal:prp:shape-products}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
\Cref{modal:thm:shape-adjoint}, \Cref{modal:thm:triple}, \Cref{modal:thm:lambda,modal:prp:shape-products}.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- rem-12: body_md -->
\label{modal:rem:string}
    Two uses. First, it identifies the two ways in which the measurable theory of \cite{For21} sits
    inside the present one, and \Cref{prob:thm:functor-unit}(3) shows that the monad commutes
    with the rigid embedding, so that \cite{For21} is recovered on the nose. Second, in a semantics
    the modalities are how non-differentiable data is typed: a value in $\flat\mathcal{S}$ cannot be
    differentiated because it cannot vary smoothly, and by \Cref{modal:thm:triple} that is a
    property of the object rather than a side condition on morphisms. We do not pursue the
    programming consequences here.
<!-- end rem-12 -->
<!-- not-3: body_md -->
\label{prob:not:law}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$, $n \ge 0$ and $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ define
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{L} Y:\; \Omega_n &\longrightarrow \mathcal{P}\left ( \mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{X}\right ) , &
        \mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) &:= \left (  \omega' \mapsto Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  \right ) _* U .
        \label{eq:law}
    \end{align}
    The seed of $Y$ is split by $\Theta$ into a \emph{parameter} half, retained as the second
    argument of $\mathsf{L} Y$, and a \emph{sampling} half, integrated out against $U$.
<!-- end not-3 -->
<!-- def-14: body_md -->
\label{prob:def:PrPf}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ put
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}) &:= \left \{  X_*P \,\middle|\, X \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega,\ P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega \right \} , &
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n} &:= \left \{  \mathsf{L} Y \,\middle|\, Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} \right \}  .
        \label{eq:PrPf-plots}
    \end{align}
<!-- end def-14 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{prob:lem:object}
    \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots} is well defined --- every value of $\mathsf{L} Y$ lies in $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$ ---
    and satisfies (P1) and (P2).
    \begin{proof}
        \emph{Values.} Fix $(t,\omega)$ and put
        $\iota := \left \langle  \mathrm{const}_t,\ \Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right \rangle $, a morphism
        $\Omega_0\to\Omega_n$ by \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, its seed part lying in
        $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$2) with \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(1). Then $Y\circ\iota$, which sends $\omega'$ to
        $Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right ) $, lies in $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$, and its law under $U$
        lies in $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$.

        \emph{(P1).} Let $\mu = X_*P \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$. By ($\Omega$5) choose
        $\psi \in \Omega^\Omega$ with $\psi_*U = P$ and put
        $Y := X\circ\psi\circ\Theta_2\circ\pi_n \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. Then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left ( \omega'\mapsto X(\psi(\omega'))\right ) _*U = X_*P = \mu$ for all
        $(t,\omega)$.

        \emph{(P2).} Let $h = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and put
        \begin{align}
            Y'(s,\sigma) &:= Y\Big( g\left (  s,\Theta_1\sigma\right ) ,\ \Theta^{-1}\big(\Phi(\Theta_1\sigma),
            \ \Theta_2\sigma\big)\Big).
            \label{eq:PrPf-substitution}
        \end{align}
        The map $(s,\sigma)\mapsto \left (  g(s,\Theta_1\sigma),\,\Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\Theta_1\sigma),
        \Theta_2\sigma)\right ) $ is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$: its smooth part satisfies
        (M1) because $g$ does and (M2) by ($\Omega$2), and its seed part is Borel and independent of
        $s$. Hence $Y' \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$. Substituting $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$, so that
        $\Theta_1\sigma = \omega$ and $\Theta_2\sigma = \omega'$, gives
        $Y'\left (  s,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  = Y\left (  g(s,\omega),\Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\omega),
        \omega')\right ) $ and therefore $\mathsf{L} Y' = \left ( \mathsf{L} Y\right ) \circ h$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-13 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
\emph{Values.} Fix $(t,\omega)$ and put
        $\iota := \left \langle  \mathrm{const}_t,\ \Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right \rangle $, a morphism
        $\Omega_0\to\Omega_n$ by \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, its seed part lying in
        $\Omega^\Omega$ by ($\Omega$2) with \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(1). Then $Y\circ\iota$, which sends $\omega'$ to
        $Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right ) $, lies in $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$, and its law under $U$
        lies in $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$.

        \emph{(P1).} Let $\mu = X_*P \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$. By ($\Omega$5) choose
        $\psi \in \Omega^\Omega$ with $\psi_*U = P$ and put
        $Y := X\circ\psi\circ\Theta_2\circ\pi_n \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. Then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left ( \omega'\mapsto X(\psi(\omega'))\right ) _*U = X_*P = \mu$ for all
        $(t,\omega)$.

        \emph{(P2).} Let $h = (g,\Phi) \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_m,\Omega_n)$ and put
        \begin{align}
            Y'(s,\sigma) &:= Y\Big( g\left (  s,\Theta_1\sigma\right ) ,\ \Theta^{-1}\big(\Phi(\Theta_1\sigma),
            \ \Theta_2\sigma\big)\Big).
            \label{eq:PrPf-substitution}
        \end{align}
        The map $(s,\sigma)\mapsto \left (  g(s,\Theta_1\sigma),\,\Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\Theta_1\sigma),
        \Theta_2\sigma)\right ) $ is a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism $\Omega_m\to\Omega_n$: its smooth part satisfies
        (M1) because $g$ does and (M2) by ($\Omega$2), and its seed part is Borel and independent of
        $s$. Hence $Y' \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_m}$. Substituting $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$, so that
        $\Theta_1\sigma = \omega$ and $\Theta_2\sigma = \omega'$, gives
        $Y'\left (  s,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  = Y\left (  g(s,\omega),\Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\omega),
        \omega')\right ) $ and therefore $\mathsf{L} Y' = \left ( \mathsf{L} Y\right ) \circ h$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- prp-17: body_md -->
\label{prob:prp:underlying}
    $\natural\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}) = \mathsf{P}(\natural\mathcal{X})$, with $\mathsf{P}$ on the right the push-forward monad of
    \Cref{qus:def:PrPf}. In particular $\mathcal{B}_{\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra of
    \cite{For21} and no measure-theoretic notion changes.
    \begin{proof}
        The underlying sets agree by \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots}. For the random variables, let
        $Y \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ and put $X(\omega) := Y\left ( \Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right ) $. Then
        $X \in \left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right ) ^\Omega$: for $\Phi,Z \in \Omega^\Omega$ the map
        $\omega\mapsto X(\Phi(\omega))(Z(\omega)) = Y\left ( \Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\omega),Z(\omega))\right ) $ is in
        $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ by \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2), which is the function-space criterion of
        \Cref{qus:thm:quasitopos}; and $\mathsf{L} Y(\omega) = X(\omega)_*U$. Conversely let
        $X \in \left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right ) ^\Omega$ and $P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$, choose $\psi$ with $\psi_*U = P$ by
        ($\Omega$5) and put $Y(\sigma) := X(\Theta_1\sigma)\left ( \psi(\Theta_2\sigma)\right ) $, which lies in
        $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ by the same criterion. Then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(\omega) = \left ( \omega'\mapsto X(\omega)(\psi(\omega'))\right ) _*U = X(\omega)_*P$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-17 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The underlying sets agree by \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots}. For the random variables, let
        $Y \in \mathcal{X}^\Omega$ and put $X(\omega) := Y\left ( \Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right ) $. Then
        $X \in \left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right ) ^\Omega$: for $\Phi,Z \in \Omega^\Omega$ the map
        $\omega\mapsto X(\Phi(\omega))(Z(\omega)) = Y\left ( \Theta^{-1}(\Phi(\omega),Z(\omega))\right ) $ is in
        $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ by \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2), which is the function-space criterion of
        \Cref{qus:thm:quasitopos}; and $\mathsf{L} Y(\omega) = X(\omega)_*U$. Conversely let
        $X \in \left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega\right ) ^\Omega$ and $P \in \mathsf{P}_\Omega$, choose $\psi$ with $\psi_*U = P$ by
        ($\Omega$5) and put $Y(\sigma) := X(\Theta_1\sigma)\left ( \psi(\Theta_2\sigma)\right ) $, which lies in
        $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$ by the same criterion. Then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(\omega) = \left ( \omega'\mapsto X(\omega)(\psi(\omega'))\right ) _*U = X(\omega)_*P$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->

\label{prob:prp:curves}
    For every $n \ge 0$,
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\mathbb{R}^n} &= \left \{  \left (  t\mapsto \left (  Y(t,-)\right ) _*U\right )  \,\middle|\, Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n} \right \}  .
        \label{eq:reparametrisable}
    \end{align}
    \begin{proof}
        ``$\subseteq$'': if $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} = \mathsf{L} Y$ then, fixing any $\omega_0$,
        $\gamma(t) = \mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega_0) = \left (  \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ where
        $\tilde Y := Y\circ\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\Theta^{-1}(\omega_0,-)\right )  \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$.
        ``$\supseteq$'': given $\tilde Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ put $Y := \tilde Y \circ \Theta_2^{(n)}$, i.e.\
        $Y(t,\sigma) := \tilde Y(t,\Theta_2\sigma)$; then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left ( \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ for every $\omega$, so $\mathsf{L} Y$ is
        $\omega$-independent and its associated $\gamma$ is the given family.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-18 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
``$\subseteq$'': if $\gamma\circ\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n} = \mathsf{L} Y$ then, fixing any $\omega_0$,
        $\gamma(t) = \mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega_0) = \left (  \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ where
        $\tilde Y := Y\circ\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\Theta^{-1}(\omega_0,-)\right )  \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$.
        ``$\supseteq$'': given $\tilde Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ put $Y := \tilde Y \circ \Theta_2^{(n)}$, i.e.\
        $Y(t,\sigma) := \tilde Y(t,\Theta_2\sigma)$; then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left ( \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ for every $\omega$, so $\mathsf{L} Y$ is
        $\omega$-independent and its associated $\gamma$ is the given family.

<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:functor-unit}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\mathsf{P}$ is an endofunctor of $\mathbf{SSS}$: for sample-smooth $f:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ the
            push-forward $\mathsf{P}(f)(\mu) := f_*\mu$ is sample-smooth, and
            $\mathsf{P}(f)\circ\mathsf{L} Y = \mathsf{L}\left (  f\circ Y\right ) $.
        \item $\delta_\mathcal{X}:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$, $x\mapsto\delta_x$, is sample-smooth and natural.
        \item $\mathsf{P}\circ\flat = \flat\circ\mathsf{P}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    \begin{proof}
        (1) $f_*\left (  X_*P\right )  = (f\circ X)_*P \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$, so $\mathsf{P}(f)$ is well defined; the
        displayed identity is immediate from \Cref{eq:law}, and $f\circ Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$.

        (2) For $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ put $Y := p\circ\Theta_1^{(n)}$, i.e.\
        $Y(t,\sigma) := p(t,\Theta_1\sigma)$, which lies in $\mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ by
        \Cref{site:not:morphisms}. Then
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left ( \omega'\mapsto p(t,\omega)\right ) _*U = \delta_{p(t,\omega)}$, so
        $\delta_\mathcal{X}\circ p = \mathsf{L} Y \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$. Naturality is
        $f_*\delta_x = \delta_{f(x)}$.

        (3) The plots of $\flat\mathcal{S}$ are the $t$-independent ones with seed part in $\mathcal{S}^\Omega$,
        and $\mathsf{L}$ of such a plot is again $t$-independent with seed part in $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{S})^\Omega$
        by \Cref{prob:prp:underlying}; conversely every plot of $\flat\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{S})$ arises this way.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-13 -->

<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
\label{prob:lem:pf-enriched}
    For all $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ the evaluation-and-push-forward map
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}) \times \mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X} &\longrightarrow \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y}), &
        (\mu,f) &\longmapsto f_*\mu,
    \end{align}
    is sample-smooth. Equivalently, push-forward is enriched over $\mathbf{SSS}$.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $\left ( \mathsf{L} Y,F\right ) $ be a plot of the source on $\Omega_n$, so $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and
        $F \in \left ( \mathcal{Y}^\mathcal{X}\right ) ^{\Omega_n}$. Put $Z(t,\sigma) := F\left (  t,\Theta_1\sigma\right ) \left (  Y(t,\sigma)\right ) $.
        Applying \Cref{eq:function-space} with $m := n$, $h := \Theta_1^{(n)}$ and $q := Y$ shows
        $Z \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$. Substituting $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$ gives
        $Z\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  = F(t,\omega)\left (  Y(t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega'))\right ) $,
        whence $\mathsf{L} Z(t,\omega) = F(t,\omega)_* \mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega)$, which is the composite in
        question.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end lem-14 -->

<!-- thm-14: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:otimes}
    The product of measures of \Cref{qus:thm:PrPf},
    \begin{align}
        \otimes:\; \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})\times\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y}) &\longrightarrow \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}), &
        (\mu,\nu) &\longmapsto \mu\otimes\nu,
    \end{align}
    defined on all of $\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}$ by \Cref{eq:otimes-section}, is sample-smooth and
    natural in $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$. No hypothesis is placed on either space.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $\left ( \mathsf{L} Y,\mathsf{L} Z\right ) $ be a plot of the source on $\Omega_n$, with $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ and
        $Z \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$. Put
        \begin{align}
            W(t,\sigma) &:= \Big( Y\big(t,\Theta^{-1}(\Theta_1\sigma,\ \Theta_1\Theta_2\sigma)\big),
            \ Z\big(t,\Theta^{-1}(\Theta_1\sigma,\ \Theta_2\Theta_2\sigma)\big)\Big).
        \end{align}
        Each component is $Y$ resp.\ $Z$ precomposed with a $\mathbb{S}$-morphism whose smooth part is
        the projection and whose seed part is Borel, so $W \in (\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{\Omega_n}$ by
        \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}. Substituting $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$,
        \begin{align}
            W\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  &= \Big(Y\big(t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\Theta_1
            \omega')\big),\ Z\big(t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\Theta_2\omega')\big)\Big),
        \end{align}
        and under $U$ the pair $(\Theta_1\omega',\Theta_2\omega')$ has law $U\otimes U$ by
        \Cref{qus:lem:split-U}. Writing $A(\omega_1) := Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega_1)\right ) $
        and $B(\omega_2) := Z\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega_2)\right ) $, the displayed map is
        $(A,B)\circ\Theta$, which lies in $(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^\Omega$; so for
        $C \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}$ the set $\left ( (A,B)\circ\Theta\right ) ^{-1}(C)$ lies in
        $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$, and $(A,B)^{-1}(C) \in \mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$ because $\Theta$ is
        an isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces, \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2). Only then may
        ($\Omega$3) be applied. So the law of the displayed map is the product of the two marginal
        laws, computed by the iterated integral \Cref{eq:otimes-section}; that is,
        $\mathsf{L} W(t,\omega) = \mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega)\otimes\mathsf{L} Z(t,\omega)$. Naturality is naturality of
        \Cref{eq:otimes-section} in $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-14 -->

<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:cor:kernel-indep}
    For all $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{Z} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ the map
    \begin{align}
        \otimes:\; \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^\mathcal{Z} \times \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z} &\longrightarrow
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z}, &
        P(X|Z)\otimes Q(Y|Z) &= \left (  P\otimes Q\right ) (X,Y|Z),
        \label{eq:kernel-indep}
    \end{align}
    given on points by $(P\otimes Q)(z) := P(z)\otimes Q(z)$, is sample-smooth.
    \begin{proof}
        By \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed} it suffices that the uncurried map
        $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^\mathcal{Z}\times\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})$,
        $(P,Q,z)\mapsto P(z)\otimes Q(z)$, be sample-smooth; it is
        $\otimes\circ(\mathrm{ev}\times\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha$ for the evident sample-smooth rearrangement
        $\alpha$, and $\mathrm{ev}$ is sample-smooth by \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end cor-2 -->

\label{prob:cor:strength}
    The costrength and the strength
    \begin{align}
        \rho_{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}}:\; \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})\times\mathcal{Y} &\to \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}), &
        (\mu,y) &\mapsto \mu\otimes\delta_y, \\
        \tau_{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}}:\; \mathcal{X}\times\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y}) &\to \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}), &
        (x,\nu) &\mapsto \delta_x\otimes\nu,
    \end{align}
    are sample-smooth and natural, and are related by the braiding.

    \end{proof}

<!-- thm-15: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:mult}
    For every $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ the mixture map
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}:\; \mathsf{P}\left ( \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})\right )  &\longrightarrow \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}), &
        \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}(\Gamma) &:= \int \nu\,\Gamma(d\nu),
    \end{align}
    is sample-smooth and natural in $\mathcal{X}$. No hypothesis is placed on $\mathcal{X}$.
    \begin{proof}
        That $\mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}$ is a well-defined map into $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$, and natural as a map of sets,
        is \Cref{qus:thm:PrPf} together with \Cref{prob:prp:underlying}.

        A plot of $\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$ on $\Omega_n$ is $\mathsf{L}\mathcal{N}$ with
        $\mathcal{N} \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$, and $\mathcal{N} = \mathsf{L} Y$ with $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, by
        \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots} applied twice. Define the Borel map
        \begin{align}
            \Psi:\;\Omega\times\Omega &\to \Omega, &
            \Psi(\omega,\tilde\omega) &:= \Theta^{-1}\Big(\Theta^{-1}\big(\omega,\Theta_1
            \tilde\omega\big),\ \Theta_2\tilde\omega\Big),
        \end{align}
        and put $Y' := Y \circ \Xi^{(n)}$ with $\Xi(\sigma) := \Psi\left ( \Theta_1\sigma,\Theta_2
        \sigma\right ) $, so that $\Xi \in \Omega^\Omega$ by \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices} and hence
        $Y' \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$. We claim
        \begin{align}
            \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X} \circ \mathsf{L}\left ( \mathsf{L} Y\right )  &= \mathsf{L} Y' ,
            \label{eq:mult-computation}
        \end{align}
        which proves the theorem.

        Fix $(t,\omega)$ and $A \in \mathcal{B}_\mathcal{X}$, and abbreviate
        $G_{\omega'}(\omega'') := Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}\big(\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega'),\omega''\big)\right ) $.
        By the change-of-variables formula for the push-forward defining
        $\mathsf{L}(\mathsf{L} Y)(t,\omega)$,
        \begin{align}
            \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}\Big(\mathsf{L}\left ( \mathsf{L} Y\right ) (t,\omega)\Big)(A)
            &= \int_\Omega \mathsf{L} Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right ) (A)\ U(d\omega')
            = \int_\Omega U\Big( G_{\omega'}^{-1}(A) \Big) U(d\omega') .
        \end{align}
        The map $G:\,(\omega',\omega'')\mapsto G_{\omega'}(\omega'')$ satisfies
        $G\circ\Theta = \left ( \omega''' \mapsto Y(t,\Psi(\omega,\omega'''))\right ) $, which lies in
        $\mathcal{X}^\Omega$, being $Y$ precomposed with the $\mathbb{S}$-morphism
        $\left \langle \mathrm{const}_t,\Psi(\omega,-)\right \rangle $. Hence $(G\circ\Theta)^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{B}_\Omega$
        and, $\Theta$ being an isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2), $G^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$. Therefore ($\Omega$3) applies and
        \begin{align}
            \int_\Omega U\Big(G_{\omega'}^{-1}(A)\Big) U(d\omega')
            &= \left (  U\otimes U\right ) \left (  G^{-1}(A)\right ) 
            = U\Big(\left (  G\circ\Theta\right ) ^{-1}(A)\Big) \nonumber \\
            &= U\Big(\left \{  \omega''' \,\middle|\, Y\left (  t,\Psi(\omega,\omega''')\right )  \in A \right \} \Big),
        \end{align}
        the middle equality by \Cref{qus:lem:split-U}. On the other hand, substituting
        $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega''')$ in the definition of $Y'$ gives
        $Y'\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega''')\right )  = Y\left (  t,\Psi(\omega,\omega''')\right ) $, so the last
        display is $\mathsf{L} Y'(t,\omega)(A)$. This is \Cref{eq:mult-computation}.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-15 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->

        is \Cref{qus:thm:PrPf} together with \Cref{prob:prp:underlying}.

        A plot of $\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$ on $\Omega_n$ is $\mathsf{L}\mathcal{N}$ with
        $\mathcal{N} \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$, and $\mathcal{N} = \mathsf{L} Y$ with $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, by

            \tilde\omega\big),\ \Theta_2\tilde\omega\Big),

        and put $Y' := Y \circ \Xi^{(n)}$ with $\Xi(\sigma) := \Psi\left ( \Theta_1\sigma,\Theta_2
        \sigma\right ) $, so that $\Xi \in \Omega^\Omega$ by \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices} and hence

            \label{eq:mult-computation}

        which proves the theorem.

        Fix $(t,\omega)$ and $A \in \mathcal{B}_\mathcal{X}$, and abbreviate
        $G_{\omega'}(\omega'') := Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}\big(\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega'),\omega''\big)\right ) $.
        By the change-of-variables formula for the push-forward defining
        $\mathsf{L}(\mathsf{L} Y)(t,\omega)$,
        \begin{align}
            \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}\Big(\mathsf{L}\left ( \mathsf{L} Y\right ) (t,\omega)\Big)(A)
            &= \int_\Omega \mathsf{L} Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right ) (A)\ U(d\omega')
            = \int_\Omega U\Big( G_{\omega'}^{-1}(A) \Big) U(d\omega') .
        \end{align}
        The map $G:\,(\omega',\omega'')\mapsto G_{\omega'}(\omega'')$ satisfies
        $G\circ\Theta = \left ( \omega''' \mapsto Y(t,\Psi(\omega,\omega'''))\right ) $, which lies in

        and, $\Theta$ being an isomorphism of quasi-universal spaces by
        \Cref{qus:lem:borel-suffices}(2), $G^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal{B}_{\Omega\times\Omega}$. Therefore ($\Omega$3) applies and
        \begin{align}
            \int_\Omega U\Big(G_{\omega'}^{-1}(A)\Big) U(d\omega')
            &= \left (  U\otimes U\right ) \left (  G^{-1}(A)\right ) 
            = U\Big(\left (  G\circ\Theta\right ) ^{-1}(A)\Big) \nonumber \\
            &= U\Big(\left \{  \omega''' \,\middle|\, Y\left (  t,\Psi(\omega,\omega''')\right )  \in A \right \} \Big),
        \end{align}
        the middle equality by \Cref{qus:lem:split-U}. On the other hand, substituting
        $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega''')$ in the definition of $Y'$ gives
        $Y'\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega''')\right )  = Y\left (  t,\Psi(\omega,\omega''')\right ) $, so the last
        display is $\mathsf{L} Y'(t,\omega)(A)$. This is \Cref{eq:mult-computation}.

<!-- thm-16: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:monad}
    $\left ( \mathsf{P},\delta,\mathbb{M}\right ) $ is a monad on $\mathbf{SSS}$, strong for the cartesian monoidal structure,
    commutative and affine. It is a genuine endofunctor of $\mathbf{SSS}$ and no subcategory, closure
    property or regularity hypothesis is involved.
    \begin{proof}
        Functor, unit and multiplication are sample-smooth by \Cref{prob:thm:functor-unit},
        \Cref{prob:thm:mult}, and all three are natural. The monad laws
        $\mathbb{M}\circ\delta_{\mathsf{P}} = \mathrm{id} = \mathbb{M}\circ\mathsf{P}(\delta)$ and
        $\mathbb{M}\circ\mathbb{M}_{\mathsf{P}} = \mathbb{M}\circ\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{M})$ are equalities of maps of underlying sets,
        which hold by \Cref{qus:thm:PrPf,prob:prp:underlying}; since a sample-smooth map
        is determined by its underlying map, they hold in $\mathbf{SSS}$.

        Strength is \Cref{prob:cor:strength}. Commutativity: both double strengths
        $\mathbb{M}\circ\mathsf{P}(\tau)\circ\rho$ and $\mathbb{M}\circ\mathsf{P}(\rho)\circ\tau$ equal $\otimes$, by the
        pointwise computation $\int\left ( \delta_x\otimes\nu\right ) \mu(dx) = \mu\otimes\nu$ and its mirror
        image, which is legitimate now that all three maps are sample-smooth; symmetry of $\otimes$
        is ($\Omega$3). Affineness is $\mathsf{P}(\mathbf{1})\cong\mathbf{1}$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-16 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->

<!-- thm-17: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:kernel-dep}
    For all $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{Z} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ the product of Markov kernels
    \begin{align}
        \otimes:\; \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Z}} \times \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z} &\longrightarrow
        \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z}, &
        K(X|Y,Z) \otimes Q(Y|Z) &= P(X,Y|Z),
        \label{eq:kernel-dep}
    \end{align}
    given on points by
    $\left (  K\otimes Q\right ) (z) = \mathbb{M}\Big(\left (  y\mapsto K(y,z)\otimes\delta_y\right ) _* Q(z)\Big)$, is
    sample-smooth. No hypothesis is placed on any of the three spaces.
    \begin{proof}
        We uncurry fully, so that $K$ and $Q$ vary with the rest. The map
        \begin{align}
            \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Z}} \times \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y}
            &\longrightarrow \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}), &
            (K,z,y) &\longmapsto \rho_{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}}\left ( \mathrm{ev}\left (  K,(y,z)\right ) ,\ y\right ) ,
        \end{align}
        is sample-smooth, being $\rho_{\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}}$ of \Cref{prob:cor:strength} precomposed with
        the evaluation of \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed} and the evident sample-smooth
        rearrangement. Currying it in $\mathcal{Y}$
        gives a sample-smooth map into $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{\mathcal{Y}}$; pairing that with
        $\mathrm{ev}:\,\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ and applying the enriched
        push-forward of \Cref{prob:lem:pf-enriched} --- which is what is needed, the map along
        which one pushes forward varying with $(K,z)$ --- followed by $\mathbb{M}$, sample-smooth by
        \Cref{prob:thm:mult}, gives a sample-smooth map
        $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Z}}\times\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}
        \to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})$. Currying in $\mathcal{Z}$ is \Cref{sss:thm:cartesian-closed}
        again, and on points the composite is the displayed formula.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-17 -->

<!-- rem-13: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:dep-free}
\Cref{eq:kernel-dep} is not an independent statement: it is \emph{equivalent} to sample-smoothness
    of $\mathbb{M}$, as one sees by taking $\mathcal{Y} := \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})$, $\mathcal{Z} := \mathbf{1}$ and $K := \mathrm{id}$, whose
    $\mathcal{X}$-marginal is $\int\nu\,Q(d\nu) = \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{X}(Q)$. So the dependent product of kernels is
    the multiplication in another guise. Here both are theorems and the equivalence is a curiosity;
    in a setting where the multiplication is problematic it says that the dependent product is
    exactly as problematic.
<!-- end rem-13 -->
<!-- thm-18: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:expectation}
    The map
    \begin{align}
        \mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}) &\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, & \mu &\longmapsto \int \cos \, d\mu,
        \label{eq:expectation-not-smooth}
    \end{align}
    is \emph{not} sample-smooth, although $\cos$ is sample-smooth, bounded, and has all derivatives
    bounded. Consequently the two-variable evaluation
    $\left (  h,\mu\right )  \mapsto \int h\,d\mu$ is not sample-smooth on
    $\mathcal{C}_b(\mathbb{R})\times\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R})$, where $\mathcal{C}_b(\mathcal{X}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\mathcal{X}$ is the subobject of
    bounded sample-smooth functions --- on which, unlike on all of $\mathbb{R}^\mathcal{X}$, the integral is
    everywhere defined.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $C(\sigma) := \tan\left ( \pi(\sigma_0-\tfrac12)\right ) $ for $\sigma_0 \in (0,1)$ and
    $C(\sigma) := 0$ for $\sigma_0 \in \left \{ 0,1\right \} $, where $\sigma_0$ is the first coordinate of
    $\sigma \in [0,1]^\mathbb{N}$. Then $C$ is Borel, so $C \in \mathbb{R}^\Omega$, and $C_*U$ is the standard
    Cauchy distribution, the exceptional set being $U$-null. Put $Y(t,\sigma) := t\,C(\Theta_2\sigma)$, which lies in $\mathbb{R}^{\Omega_1}$, being
    smooth in $t$ and Borel in $\sigma$. Then $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega)$ is the law $\mu_t$ of $t\,C$ for
    every $\omega$, so $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is an admissible curve of $\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R})$ by
    \Cref{prob:prp:curves}. But
    \begin{align}
        \int \cos \, d\mu_t &= \mathbb{E}\left [ \cos(tC)\right ]  = e^{-\left|  t\right| },
    \end{align}
    the characteristic function of the Cauchy distribution, which is not differentiable at $t = 0$.
        The second claim follows by precomposing with the sample-smooth map
        $\mu\mapsto(\cos,\mu)$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-18 -->

<!-- rem-14: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:expectation}
    So $\mathsf{P}$ is a monad whose objects carry smooth families along which expectations of perfectly
    ordinary functions fail to be smooth. This is not an artefact of \Cref{prob:def:PrPf}: the curve
    in the proof of \Cref{prob:thm:expectation} is the law of a smoothly varying random variable, so
    any notion of smooth family that contains the reparametrisable ones contains it. What it says is
    that a \emph{second}, expectation-based structure is genuinely different from this one, not a
    refinement of it; see \Cref{disc:sec:open}. It also says that the loss function of a variational
    program is in general not interpreted by the structure that interprets the program, and
    \Cref{sec:ml} is where that gap is bridged, by an analytic hypothesis rather than a categorical
    one.
<!-- end rem-14 -->
<!-- def-15: body_md -->
\label{prob:def:kleisli}
    $\mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})$ has the objects of $\mathbf{SSS}$ and $\mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}) :=
    \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathcal{X},\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})\right ) $, with composition
    $L \bullet K := \mathbb{M}_\mathcal{Z}\circ\mathsf{P}(L)\circ K$ and identities $\delta$. We call it the category
    of \emph{differentiable simulators}: by \Cref{prob:thm:representation} every morphism is, plot
    by plot, a smoothly parametrised sampler, and by \Cref{prob:cor:sampler-bijection} the morphisms
    out of $\mathbb{R}^m$ are exactly the samplers, taken up to equality of law at each parameter value.
<!-- end def-15 -->
<!-- thm-19: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:markov}
    $\mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})$ is a symmetric monoidal category with $\mathcal{X}\otimes\mathcal{Y} :=
    \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ and unit $\mathbf{1}$, in which every object carries the commutative comonoid
    \begin{align}
        \left ( \mathrm{copy}_\mathcal{X},\ \mathrm{del}_\mathcal{X}\right )  &:= \left (  \delta\circ\Delta_\mathcal{X},\
        \delta\circ !_\mathcal{X} \right ) ,
    \end{align}
    compatibly with the monoidal structure, and in which $\mathbf{1}$ is terminal --- equivalently,
    $\mathrm{del}$ is natural. That is, $\mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})$ is a Markov category in the sense of
    \cite{Fri20}, for every object of $\mathbf{SSS}$ and with no further hypothesis. It is not cartesian:
    $\mathrm{copy}$ is not natural, since for a non-Dirac $\mu \in \mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R})$ one has
    $\Delta_*\mu \ne \mu\otimes\mu$. It \emph{is} natural along every morphism in the image of
    the functor $\delta_*:\,\mathbf{SSS}\to\mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})$, so every such morphism is deterministic in
    the sense of \cite{Fri20}; whether the converse holds for a given $\mathcal{Y}$ depends on
    $\mathcal{B}_\mathcal{Y}$ being countably separating, and we do not pursue it.
    \begin{proof}
        By \Cref{prob:thm:monad} the monad is strong, commutative and affine on the cartesian
        monoidal category $\mathbf{SSS}$; the Kleisli category of such a monad is a Markov category, see
        \cite{Fri20}. Concretely, the monoidal product of $K:\,\mathcal{X}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ and
        $L:\,\mathcal{Z}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{W})$ is $K\boxtimes L := \otimes\circ(K\times L)$, which is
        sample-smooth by \Cref{prob:thm:otimes} and functorial by commutativity; the comonoid
        laws are the identities that $\Delta$ and $!$ satisfy in $\mathbf{SSS}$, transported along
        $\delta_*$; and terminality of $\mathbf{1}$, i.e.\ naturality of $\mathrm{del}$, is affineness.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-19 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->

<!-- rem-15: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:conditionals}
    \Cref{prob:thm:markov} gives a Markov category and nothing beyond it. The further structure one
    may ask of a Markov category is not addressed here and is left to a sequel. The reason for
    stopping is worth stating, because it is the distinction that runs through the whole paper: the
    present construction removes the \emph{selection} problems, those of choosing a representative
    measurably, and the multiplication was one of them; it does nothing about problems of
    \emph{inverting} a push-forward, and no choice of plots can.
<!-- end rem-15 -->
<!-- thm-20: body_md -->
\label{prob:thm:representation}
    Let $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ and let $K \in \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathcal{X},\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})\right ) $ be a Kleisli morphism.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For every $n$ and every $p \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ there is $Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$ with
            \begin{align}
                K\left (  p(t,\omega)\right )  &= \left (  \omega'\mapsto Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right ) \right ) _*U
                \qquad\text{for all } (t,\omega).
            \end{align}
        \item In particular, for $\mathcal{X} := \mathbb{R}^m$ every sample-smooth $K:\,\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ is of
            the form $K(t) = \left (  Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ with $Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$; that is, $K$ is a
            \emph{reparametrisation}, jointly smooth in the parameter and measurable in the seed.
        \item Representations compose: if $K$ is represented by $Y$ on the plot $p$ and
            $L:\,\mathcal{Y}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{W})$ is any Kleisli morphism, then $L\bullet K$ is represented on
            $p$ by some $W \in \mathcal{W}^{\Omega_n}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    \begin{proof}
        (1) $K\circ p \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^{\Omega_n} = \left \{ \mathsf{L} Y \,\middle|\, Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}\right \} $ by
        \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots}. (2) Apply (1) to $p := \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m} \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^m\right ) ^{\Omega_m}$ and evaluate at a fixed
        $\omega_0$, using \Cref{prob:prp:curves}. (3) $L\bullet K$ is a Kleisli morphism, so (1)
        applies to it.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-20 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
(1) $K\circ p \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^{\Omega_n} = \left \{ \mathsf{L} Y \,\middle|\, Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}\right \} $ by
        \Cref{eq:PrPf-plots}. (2) Apply (1) to $p := \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^m} \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^m\right ) ^{\Omega_m}$ and evaluate at a fixed
        $\omega_0$, using \Cref{prob:prp:curves}. (3) $L\bullet K$ is a Kleisli morphism, so (1)
        applies to it.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- prp-19: body_md -->
\label{prob:prp:sampler-to-kernel}
    Let $\mathcal{W},\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbf{SSS}$ and let $F \in \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathcal{W}\times\flat\Omega,\ \mathcal{Y}\right ) $ be a
    \emph{sampler}. Then
    \begin{align}
        \widetilde F:\; \mathcal{W} \longrightarrow \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y}), \qquad
        \widetilde F(w) &:= \left (  F(w,-)\right ) _*U,
    \end{align}
    is a Kleisli morphism, and $\widetilde F$ depends on $F$ only through the laws
    $\left (  F(w,-)\right ) _*U$.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $q \in \mathcal{W}^{\Omega_n}$ and put
        \begin{align}
            Y(t,\sigma) &:= F\left (  q(t,\Theta_1\sigma),\ \Theta_2\sigma\right )  .
        \end{align}
        The pair $(t,\sigma)\mapsto\left (  q(t,\Theta_1\sigma),\Theta_2\sigma\right ) $ is a plot
        of $\mathcal{W}\times\flat\Omega$ on $\Omega_n$: its first component is $q\circ\Theta_1^{(n)}$,
        a plot by \Cref{site:not:morphisms}, and its second is $\Theta_2\circ\pi_n$, a plot of
        $\flat\Omega$ by \Cref{sss:eg:flat-sharp} since $\Theta_2 \in \Omega^\Omega$. As $F$ is
        sample-smooth, $Y \in \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_n}$. Substituting
        $\sigma := \Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')$ gives
        $Y\left (  t,\Theta^{-1}(\omega,\omega')\right )  = F\left (  q(t,\omega),\omega'\right ) $, so
        $\mathsf{L} Y(t,\omega) = \left (  F(q(t,\omega),-)\right ) _*U = \widetilde F\left (  q(t,\omega)\right ) $; that is,
        $\widetilde F \circ q = \mathsf{L} Y$, which lies in $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})^{\Omega_n}$. The last clause is
        immediate from the formula.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-19 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->

        The pair $(t,\sigma)\mapsto\left (  q(t,\Theta_1\sigma),\Theta_2\sigma\right ) $ is a plot

        immediate from the formula.
