<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{prob:cor:sampler-bijection}
    $\Omega_m \cong \mathbb{R}^m\times\flat\Omega$ in $\mathbf{SSS}$, so that a sampler
    $\mathbb{R}^m\times\flat\Omega\to\mathcal{Y}$ is the same thing as an element of $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$; and the
    law map $Y \mapsto \left ( \theta\mapsto\left (  Y(\theta,-)\right ) _*U\right ) $ induces a bijection
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}\big/\!\!\sim \;\;\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\;\; \mathrm{Kl}(\mathsf{P})\left ( \mathbb{R}^m,\mathcal{Y}\right ) , &&
        Y \sim Y' \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; \left (  Y(\theta,-)\right ) _*U = \left (  Y'(\theta,-)\right ) _*U
        \ \ \forall\theta .
    \end{align}
    \begin{proof}
        For the isomorphism, both objects have underlying set $\mathbb{R}^m\times\Omega$ and, by
        \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod}, \Cref{sss:eg:euclidean,sss:eg:flat-sharp},
        \begin{align}
            \left ( \mathbb{R}^m\times\flat\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &= \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_n,\mathbb{R}^m) \times
            \left \{  \Phi\circ\pi_n \,\middle|\, \Phi \in \Omega^\Omega\right \}  = \mathbb{S}(\Omega_n,\Omega_m)
            = \Omega_m^{\Omega_n},
        \end{align}
        the last equality by \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}. The law map is well defined by
        \Cref{prob:prp:sampler-to-kernel}, surjective by \Cref{prob:thm:representation}(2), and its
        fibres are the $\sim$-classes by construction.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end cor-4 -->

            \left ( \mathbb{R}^m\times\flat\Omega\right ) ^{\Omega_n} &= \mathcal{C}^\infty_{\mathrm{mix}}(\Omega_n,\mathbb{R}^m) \times

            = \Omega_m^{\Omega_n},
        \end{align}
        the last equality by \Cref{sss:lem:plots-are-homs}. The law map is well defined by

<!-- rem-16: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:reparam}
    \Cref{prob:thm:representation} is the statement that underlies the reparametrisation gradient of
    the machine-learning literature: a smooth family of distributions is the law of a smoothly
    varying random variable, so that --- under the integrability hypothesis (D) of
    \Cref{ml:thm:pathwise}, which \Cref{prob:thm:expectation} shows cannot be dropped ---
    $\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_{\mu_\theta}[h]$ may be computed by differentiating inside the
    expectation. In a setting where a smooth family of measures is
    defined by a condition rather than by a representation, this is a genuine theorem to be proved,
    and not an easy one. Here it holds by construction and is closed under Kleisli composition, part
    (3) --- which is the property a semantics actually needs, since a program is a composite. The
    honest accounting is that nothing has been proved about representability: we have chosen a
    category in which the smooth families are the represented ones, and \Cref{prob:rem:comparison}
    says what that choice excludes.
<!-- end rem-16 -->
<!-- rem-17: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:three-levels}
    Three properties are easily run together, and it is worth keeping them apart.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(L1)] \emph{Denoting.} The program is a morphism $\mathcal{X}\to\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{Y})$: it names a
            distribution.
        \item[(L2)] \emph{Sampling.} That distribution is the law of $f(x,\omega)$ for some
            \emph{measurable} $f$.
        \item[(L3)] \emph{Sampling smoothly.} Such an $f$ may be found which is in addition smooth
            in $x$, i.e.\ which lies in $\mathcal{Y}^{\Omega_m}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Level (L2) is classical and nearly free: on a standard Borel space the quantile transform
    produces such an $f$. Level (L3) is \Cref{prob:thm:representation}, and it is what the pathwise
    gradient of \Cref{ml:thm:pathwise} consumes. The two are not the same, and the quantile
    transform is already the illustration: it is a step function for a discrete family, so it
    witnesses (L2) while saying nothing about (L3).

    Here is the failure in the present setting. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the two-point quasi-universal space
    whose random variables are all measurable maps $\Omega\to\left \{ 0,1\right \} $, and consider the Bernoulli
    family $\theta\mapsto\mathrm{Ber}(\theta)$ with values in $\mathsf{P}\left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right ) $. Level (L2)
    holds, since $f(\theta,\omega) := \mathds{1}\left [ \omega_0\le\theta\right ] $ is jointly measurable, $\omega_0$
    being the first coordinate, and $\mathrm{Ber}(\theta) = \left (  f(\theta,-)\right ) _*U$. Level (L3)
    fails: every $Y \in \left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right ) ^{\Omega_1}$ is independent of $\theta$ by
    \Cref{sss:eg:flat-sharp}, so $\left (  Y(\theta,-)\right ) _*U$ is constant in $\theta$, whereas
    $\mathrm{Ber}(\theta)$ is not. Equivalently, by \Cref{prob:thm:functor-unit}(3) the object
    $\mathsf{P}\left ( \flat\mathcal{S}\right )  = \flat\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{S})$ is rigid and admits no non-constant curve at all.

    Two readings, both worth having. First, (L3) is a property of the family \emph{together with
    the structure on the target}, not of the family alone: the same Bernoulli family does satisfy
    (L3) into the loose object $\sharp\mathcal{S}$, by $Y(\theta,\sigma) := \mathds{1}\left [ (\Theta_2\sigma)_0 \le
    \theta\right ] $, every substitution of which is a measurable indicator. Second, nothing is gained
    that way, because $\mathbf{SSS}\left ( \sharp\mathcal{S},\mathbb{R}\right ) $ consists of the constants alone --- the map
    $(t,\omega)\mapsto\mathds{1}\left [  t>0\right ] $ is a plot of $\sharp\mathcal{S}$, and a morphism to $\mathbb{R}$ would carry
    it to a step function, which is not a plot of $\mathbb{R}$ --- so no expectation downstream could be
    differentiated. This is why the standard remedy for a discrete latent is a genuinely smooth
    relaxation and not a coarser structure, \Cref{ml:sec:nonsmooth}.
<!-- end rem-17 -->
<!-- prp-20: body_md -->
\label{prob:prp:necessary}
    Every $p \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$ satisfies
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $p(-,\omega) \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\mathbb{R}^n}$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$, and
        \item $p\circ h \in \mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^\Omega$ for every $h \in \mathbb{S}(\Omega_0,\Omega_n)$;
    \end{enumerate}
    that is, $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n} \subseteq \widehat{\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})}^{\Omega_n}$ in the notation of
    \Cref{eq:maximal-extension}.
    \begin{proof}
        (2) is (P2). For (1), $p = \mathsf{L} Y$ and
        $p(t,\omega) = \left ( \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ with
        $\tilde Y := Y\circ\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right )  \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, so
        \Cref{prob:prp:curves} applies.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-20 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
(2) is (P2). For (1), $p = \mathsf{L} Y$ and
        $p(t,\omega) = \left ( \tilde Y(t,-)\right ) _*U$ with
        $\tilde Y := Y\circ\left ( \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{R}^n},\Theta^{-1}(\omega,-)\right )  \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$, so
        \Cref{prob:prp:curves} applies.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- rem-18: body_md -->
\label{prob:rem:comparison}
    The converse of \Cref{prob:prp:necessary} asks: given a family $\mathcal{N}$ of measures which is a
    smooth family for each fixed seed and an admissible random measure for each fixed substitution,
    produce a single $Y \in \mathcal{X}^{\Omega_n}$ representing it. That is a measurable selection
    problem --- one must choose a representative of $\mathcal{N}(t,\omega)$ measurably in $\omega$ and
    smoothly in $t$ at once. Selections of Jankov--von Neumann type \cite{Kec95} return universally
    measurable functions, and universal measurability is exactly what ($\Omega$4) makes admissible;
    but they give no control in the $t$-direction, which is the whole difficulty, so they do not by
    themselves settle anything here. Whether the selection can be made we do not know, and nothing
    above depends on the answer.

    That is the point of the arrangement. Had objects been built from a pair
    $\left ( \mathcal{X}^\Omega,\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{R}}\right ) $, the mixed family would have been \emph{forced} to be
    $\widehat{\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})}^{\Omega_1}$ while the monad needs $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_1}$, so the
    multiplication would exist only where the two agree --- over a subcategory, and only relatively.
    Here the mixed family is primitive and is defined to be the image. The difficulty is therefore
    not dissolved but relocated, out of the existence of the monad and into the question of whether
    the inclusion of \Cref{prob:prp:necessary} is an equality; and that question is now inert.

    Two consequences of the choice should be stated plainly. First, by
    \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice} an object of $\mathbf{SSS}$ is not presented by its curves and its
    random variables: the mixed family is separate data, and the price of \Cref{sss:rem:no-boman} is
    paid at exactly this point. Second, wherever the inclusion is strict
    a Kleisli morphism must come with a representation, so there are fewer of them than a
    curve-and-random-variable presentation would admit; \Cref{prob:thm:representation}(3) says that
    this is nevertheless a well-behaved class, closed under composition.
<!-- end rem-18 -->
<!-- thm-21: body_md -->
\label{ml:thm:pathwise}
    Let $Y \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^d\right ) ^{\Omega_q}$, let $\mu_\theta := \left (  Y(\theta,-)\right ) _*U$, and let
    $h \in \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}\right )  = C^\infty\left ( \mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}\right ) $ be bounded with $\nabla h$ bounded. Assume
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(D)] for every compact $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^q$ there is a $U$-integrable
            $B_K:\,\Omega\to\left [ 0,\infty\right ] $ such that
            $\sup_{\theta\in K}\left\|  \partial_\theta Y(\theta,\omega)\right\|  \le B_K(\omega)$
            holds for all $\omega \in \Omega$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $\theta \mapsto \int h\,d\mu_\theta$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^q$, with
    \begin{align}
        \nabla_\theta \int h \, d\mu_\theta &= \int_\Omega \partial_\theta Y(\theta,\omega)^\top\,
        \nabla h\left (  Y(\theta,\omega)\right )  \; U(d\omega).
        \label{eq:pathwise}
    \end{align}
    \begin{proof}
        By the change of variables formula $F(\theta) := \int h\,d\mu_\theta = \int_\Omega
        h\left (  Y(\theta,\omega)\right ) \,U(d\omega)$, the integrand being bounded and, by (M2) of
        \Cref{site:def:site} together with continuity of $h$, measurable; so $F$ is well defined.
        Put
        \begin{align}
            G_i(\theta,\omega) &:= \nabla h\left (  Y(\theta,\omega)\right ) ^\top
            \partial_{\theta_i} Y(\theta,\omega) .
        \end{align}
        Each $G_i$ is measurable in $\omega$, since $\partial_\theta Y$ is a pointwise limit of the
        difference quotients $\omega\mapsto k\left (  Y(\theta+e_i/k,\omega)-Y(\theta,\omega)\right ) $, each
        admissible by (M2), and $\nabla h$ is continuous; it is continuous in $\theta$ by (M1); and
        on a compact $K$ it is bounded by $\sup_{\mathbb{R}^d}\left\| \nabla h\right\|  \cdot B_K$, which is
        $U$-integrable by (D). In particular the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:pathwise} exists.

        Fix $\theta_0$ and let $K$ be a closed ball around it, so that $K$ is convex. For
        $\theta_0+se_i \in K$ with $s \ne 0$ the map $\varphi(s) := h\left (  Y(\theta_0+se_i,\omega)\right ) $
        is $C^1$ by (M1) and the chain rule, with $\varphi'(s) = G_i(\theta_0+se_i,\omega)$, so the
        mean value theorem applied along the segment, which lies in $K$, gives
        \begin{align}
            \frac{\left|  \varphi(s) - \varphi(0)\right| }{\left|  s \right| } &\le
            \sup\nolimits_{\mathbb{R}^d}\left\| \nabla h\right\|  \cdot B_K(\omega),
        \end{align}
        a bound independent of $s$ and $U$-integrable. Dominated convergence along any sequence
        $s\to0$ therefore gives $\partial_{\theta_i}F(\theta_0) = \int G_i(\theta_0,\omega)\,
        U(d\omega)$, which is \Cref{eq:pathwise} componentwise. The same dominating function, with
        dominated convergence applied to $\theta\mapsto G_i(\theta,\omega)$, shows that
        $\theta\mapsto\int G_i(\theta,\omega)\,U(d\omega)$ is continuous on $K$. So every partial
        derivative of $F$ exists and is continuous, and $F$ is $C^1$.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end thm-21 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->

        Put

<!-- rem-19: body_md -->
\label{ml:rem:necessity}
    Condition (D) cannot be dropped. The proof of \Cref{prob:thm:expectation} exhibits, in the present
    normalisation, $Y(t,\sigma) = t\,C(\sigma)$
    with $C$ Cauchy and $h = \cos$ --- bounded, with all derivatives bounded --- for which
    $\int h\,d\mu_t = e^{-\left|  t\right| }$ is not differentiable at $0$. There
    $\partial_t Y(t,\omega) = C(\omega)$ is not $U$-integrable, which is exactly the failure of (D).
    So the split is clean: the \emph{representation} of a family as a reparametrisation is
    categorical and free, \Cref{prob:thm:representation}; the \emph{estimator} is analysis and costs
    an integrability hypothesis.
<!-- end rem-19 -->
<!-- rem-20: body_md -->
\label{ml:rem:not-a-morphism}
    \Cref{ml:thm:pathwise} concludes that $F(\theta) = \int h\,d\mu_\theta$ is $C^1$. Nothing in
    it makes $F$ a morphism of $\mathbf{SSS}$: a morphism $\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}$ is a $C^\infty$ map by
    \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean}, whereas without hypothesis (D) the composite
    $\theta\mapsto\mu_\theta\mapsto\int h\,d\mu_\theta$ need not even be $C^1$,
    \Cref{prob:thm:expectation}, and this for $h$ bounded with all derivatives bounded. Whether (D)
    alone forces more than $C^1$ we do not address. So in general the tangent functor and
    differentials of \Cref{sss:sec:tangent} do not apply to $F$.

    What \emph{is} a morphism, and what \Cref{sss:sec:tangent} does differentiate, is the sampler:
    $Y \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^d\right ) ^{\Omega_q} = \mathbf{SSS}\left ( \Omega_q,\mathbb{R}^d\right ) $ is a plot,
    $\theta\mapsto Y(\theta,\omega)$ is a smooth family for each seed, and by
    \Cref{tan:thm:euclidean} its differential is the classical $\partial_\theta Y$.
    \Cref{eq:pathwise} is the
    statement that the gradient of the objective is the $U$-average of the differential of the
    sampler; the categorical content is on the right-hand side, the analytic hypothesis is what
    licenses the equality. This is the precise sense in which the reparametrisation gradient is
    ``differentiating the sampler rather than the objective'', and it is why an automatic
    differentiator applied to such a program is on solid ground while the objective it reports is
    not, by itself, a morphism.
<!-- end rem-20 -->
<!-- eg-5: body_md -->
\label{ml:eg:location-scale}
    Let $Z \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^d\right ) ^\Omega$ with $\mathbb{E}\left\|  Z\right\|  < \infty$, and let
    $m \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^q,\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $S \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^q,\mathbb{R}^{d\times d})$. Then
    $Y(\theta,\omega) := m(\theta) + S(\theta)\,Z(\omega)$ lies in $\left ( \mathbb{R}^d\right ) ^{\Omega_q}$ and
    satisfies (D), since $\partial_\theta Y$ is bounded on compacta by
    $c_K\left (  1 + \left\|  Z(\omega)\right\| \right ) $. Taking $Z$ standard normal, this covers the Gaussian
    family $\mu_\theta = \mathrm{N}\left (  m(\theta),\,S(\theta)S(\theta)^\top\right ) $ and hence the standard
    reparametrisation of \cite{KW14,RMW14}. Families with no closed-form reparametrisation, such as
    the Gamma, are handled by implicit differentiation of the distribution function \cite{FMM18};
    that is a statement about how to \emph{compute} $\partial_\theta Y$, not about whether $Y$
    exists, which is \Cref{prob:thm:representation}.

    An objective such as the evidence lower bound has a parameter in the integrand as well,
    $\theta \mapsto \int h(\theta,x)\,\mu_\theta(dx)$. This is the same theorem applied to
    $\widetilde Y(\theta,\omega) := \left ( \theta,\,Y(\theta,\omega)\right )  \in
    \left ( \mathbb{R}^{q+d}\right ) ^{\Omega_q}$, whose law is $\delta_\theta\otimes\mu_\theta$, and to $h$ read as a
    function on $\mathbb{R}^{q+d}$ --- so that $h$ must now be bounded with bounded gradient \emph{jointly}
    in $(\theta,x)$, a real restriction and not a formality, since the integrand of an evidence
    lower bound is typically unbounded in both arguments. Under it, \Cref{eq:pathwise} returns both
    terms,
    \begin{align}
        \nabla_\theta \int h(\theta,x)\,\mu_\theta(dx) &= \int_\Omega \Big[
        \nabla_\theta h\left ( \theta,Y(\theta,\omega)\right )  + \partial_\theta Y(\theta,\omega)^\top
        \nabla_x h\left ( \theta,Y(\theta,\omega)\right )  \Big]\, U(d\omega),
    \end{align}
    since $\partial_\theta\widetilde Y = \left ( \mathrm{id},\partial_\theta Y\right ) $ satisfies (D) whenever
    $\partial_\theta Y$ does, with dominating function $\sqrt{q} + B_K$.
<!-- end eg-5 -->
<!-- rem-21: body_md -->
\label{ml:rem:composition}
    A probabilistic program is not one sampling step but a composite of them, and the reason to
    insist on \Cref{prob:thm:monad} rather than on a single representation theorem is
    \Cref{prob:thm:representation}(3): Kleisli composition of representable families is again
    representable, because a composite of morphisms is a morphism. Concretely, if
    $K:\,\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ draws a latent and $L:\,\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}^e)$ draws an observation from
    it, then $L\bullet K$ is again of the form $\left (  W(\theta,-)\right ) _*U$ with
    $W \in \left ( \mathbb{R}^e\right ) ^{\Omega_q}$, obtained by seed splitting; one may then apply
    \Cref{ml:thm:pathwise} to the composite. Neither the representation nor its stability under
    composition carries a hypothesis. Condition (D), on the other hand, has to be checked for the
    composite, and is not implied by (D) for the two factors.
    \Cref{ml:eg:composite} carries all of this out.
<!-- end rem-21 -->
<!-- eg-6: body_md -->
\label{ml:eg:composite}
    Fix $m,s \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^q,\mathbb{R})$ with $s > 0$, a link $g \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ and $\tau > 0$, and
    let $Z \in \mathbb{R}^\Omega$ be standard normal --- say $Z(\omega) := F_{\mathrm{N}}^{-1}(\omega_0)$ for
    $\omega_0 \in (0,1)$ and $Z(\omega) := 0$ otherwise, where $F_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the standard normal
    distribution function and $\omega_0$ is the first coordinate of $\omega$. Consider the two
    stages
    \begin{align}
        K:\;\mathbb{R}^q \to \mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}), & \qquad K(\theta) := \mathrm{N}\left (  m(\theta),\,s(\theta)^2\right ) , \\
        L:\;\mathbb{R} \to \mathsf{P}(\mathbb{R}), & \qquad L(z) := \mathrm{N}\left (  g(z),\,\tau^2\right ) ,
    \end{align}
    a latent drawn from a parametrised Gaussian and an observation drawn given the latent.

    \emph{Each stage is a Kleisli morphism.} Put
    \begin{align}
        F_K(\theta,\omega) &:= m(\theta) + s(\theta)\,Z(\omega), &
        F_L(z,\omega) &:= g(z) + \tau\,Z(\omega).
    \end{align}
    Both are sample-smooth on $\mathbb{R}^q\times\flat\Omega$ resp.\ $\mathbb{R}\times\flat\Omega$, being smooth in
    the first argument and Borel in the second, and their laws are $K$ and $L$; so $K$ and $L$ are
    Kleisli morphisms by \Cref{prob:prp:sampler-to-kernel}. Nothing has been checked beyond
    smoothness of $m,s,g$ and measurability of $Z$.

    \emph{The composite, and its sampler.} By \Cref{prob:thm:representation}(3) the Kleisli
    composite $L \bullet K$ is again a sampler, and the proof of \Cref{prob:thm:mult} says which
    one: run the first stage on one half of the seed and the second on the other. Explicitly, put
    \begin{align}
        W(\theta,\omega) &:= F_L\Big( F_K\left ( \theta,\Theta_1\omega\right ) ,\ \Theta_2\omega \Big)
        = g\Big( m(\theta) + s(\theta)\,Z\left ( \Theta_1\omega\right )  \Big)
        + \tau\,Z\left ( \Theta_2\omega\right )  .
        \label{eq:composite-sampler}
    \end{align}
    Then $W \in \mathbb{R}^{\Omega_q}$, being smooth in $\theta$ and Borel in $\omega$, and
    $\left (  W(\theta,-)\right ) _*U = \left (  L\bullet K\right ) (\theta)$. Indeed $Z\circ\Theta_1$ and
    $Z\circ\Theta_2$ are independent standard normals by \Cref{qus:lem:split-U}, so under $U$ the
    variable $z := m(\theta)+s(\theta)\,Z(\Theta_1\omega)$ has law $K(\theta)$ and, given it,
    $W(\theta,\omega)$ has law $\mathrm{N}\left (  g(z),\tau^2\right )  = L(z)$; integrating out $z$ is
    $\mathbb{M}$, and gives $\int L(z)\,K(\theta)(dz) = \left (  L\bullet K\right ) (\theta)$.

    \emph{The gradient.} Assume in addition that $g'$ is bounded, and let $h \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ be
    bounded with $h'$ bounded. Then
    \begin{align}
        \partial_\theta W(\theta,\omega) &= g'\Big( m(\theta)+s(\theta)Z(\Theta_1\omega)\Big)
        \Big( \nabla m(\theta) + \nabla s(\theta)\,Z(\Theta_1\omega)\Big),
    \end{align}
    which on a compact $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^q$ is bounded by
    $c_K \left\|  g'\right\| _\infty \left (  1 + \left|  Z(\Theta_1\omega)\right| \right ) $, a $U$-integrable function since
    $\mathbb{E}\left|  Z\right|  < \infty$. So (D) holds and \Cref{ml:thm:pathwise} applies to the composite:
    \begin{align}
        \nabla_\theta \int h \, d\left (  L\bullet K\right ) (\theta) &= \int_\Omega
        h'\left (  W(\theta,\omega)\right ) \, \partial_\theta W(\theta,\omega)\; U(d\omega),
    \end{align}
    which is what an implementation computes when it draws the two seed halves once and
    differentiates the arithmetic of \Cref{eq:composite-sampler}.

    \emph{(D) is not inherited.} Take $p = 1$, $m(\theta) := \theta$, $s :\equiv 1$ and
    $g(z) := e^{z^2}$. Each stage satisfies (D): $\partial_\theta F_K \equiv 1$, and
    $\partial_z F_L = g'$ is bounded on compacta. The composite does not, since at $\theta = 0$
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}\left|  \partial_\theta W \right|  &= \mathbb{E}\left|  g'(Z)\right|  = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
        \int_\mathbb{R} \left|  z\right| \, e^{z^2/2}\,dz = \infty .
    \end{align}
    The representation composed; the integrability hypothesis did not. This is the division of
    labour of \Cref{ml:rem:necessity}, seen in a program.
<!-- end eg-6 -->
<!-- def-16: body_md -->
\label{ml:def:branched}
    Let $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}} := \left ( -\infty,0\right )  \sqcup \left [ 0,\infty\right ) $ be the coproduct in
    $\mathbf{SSS}$ of the two subobjects of $\mathbb{R}$, so that its underlying set is again $\mathbb{R}$ and, by
    \Cref{sss:prp:prod-coprod},
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}^{\Omega_n} &= \left \{  p \in \mathbb{R}^{\Omega_n} \,\middle|\, p < 0 \text{ everywhere}
        \right \}  \;\cup\; \left \{  p \in \mathbb{R}^{\Omega_n} \,\middle|\, p \ge 0 \text{ everywhere} \right \}  .
    \end{align}
<!-- end def-16 -->
<!-- prp-21: body_md -->
\label{ml:prp:relu}
    The map $\max(-,0):\,\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}\to\mathbb{R}$ is sample-smooth, with derivative $0$ on the
    open summand and $1$ on the closed one. The identity $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}\to\mathbb{R}$ is sample-smooth
    but not an isomorphism. Moreover no admissible curve of $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$ approaches the kink
    at non-zero speed from inside the closed summand: if $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}^\mathbb{R}$ takes
    values in $\left [ 0,\infty\right ) $ and $\gamma(t_0) = 0$, then $\gamma'(t_0) = 0$.
    \begin{proof}
        A plot of $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$ lands in one summand by \Cref{ml:def:branched}, and
        $\max(-,0)$ restricts on the two summands to the constant $0$ and to the identity, both
        smooth; so it carries plots to plots. The identity is sample-smooth because every plot of
        $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$ is a plot of $\mathbb{R}$, and its inverse is not, because a smooth curve
        crossing $0$ --- say $\gamma(t) = t$ --- is a plot of $\mathbb{R}$ and not of
        $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$. For the last claim, $\gamma$ attains its minimum at $t_0$ and is
        differentiable there.
    \end{proof}
<!-- end prp-21 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
A plot of $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$ lands in one summand by \Cref{ml:def:branched}, and
        $\max(-,0)$ restricts on the two summands to the constant $0$ and to the identity, both
        smooth; so it carries plots to plots. The identity is sample-smooth because every plot of
        $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$ is a plot of $\mathbb{R}$, and its inverse is not, because a smooth curve
        crossing $0$ --- say $\gamma(t) = t$ --- is a plot of $\mathbb{R}$ and not of
        $\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{br}}$. For the last claim, $\gamma$ attains its minimum at $t_0$ and is
        differentiable there.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- rem-22: body_md -->
\label{disc:rem:ledger}
    Gained: an unconditional probability monad, \Cref{prob:thm:monad}, with an unconditional Markov
    Kleisli category, \Cref{prob:thm:markov}, an unconditional dependent product of kernels,
    \Cref{prob:thm:kernel-dep}, and an unconditional representation theorem,
    \Cref{prob:thm:representation}; the compatibility axiom relating smoothness and measurability
    becomes a consequence, \Cref{sss:lem:Q4}; and Euclidean and manifold correctness become
    immediate, \Cref{sss:thm:euclidean,sss:thm:manifolds}, so that Boman's theorem
    disappears from the foundations.

    Lost: an object is no longer \emph{presented} by its curves and its random variables,
    \Cref{sss:rem:curves-do-not-suffice}, so the economy of a two-family definition is gone and
    every construction is indexed by an arity; and, wherever the inclusion of
    \Cref{prob:prp:necessary} is strict, there are fewer Kleisli morphisms than a two-family
    presentation would give, \Cref{prob:rem:comparison}. Unchanged: the measurable half, \Cref{prob:prp:underlying}, the
    smooth families, \Cref{prob:prp:curves}, and hence every concrete computation that either
    theory can express.
<!-- end rem-22 -->
<!-- rem-23: body_md -->
\label{disc:rem:locality}
    We do not impose a sheaf condition, and \Cref{site:rem:no-locality} explains that this is a
    choice rather than an oversight. It is worth saying what each side of the choice is for.

    Locality --- test objects $V\times\Omega$ for open $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and plots required to be local
    in the smooth direction --- buys \emph{gluing}: constructing a morphism from local pieces, and
    constructing an object from local data. That is what differential-geometric arguments on objects
    which are not manifolds need: de Rham theory, integration of forms, connections, bundles
    presented by transition functions. It is \emph{not} needed for tangent and cotangent spaces, for
    Jacobians, or for classical differential geometry on manifolds, which by
    \Cref{sss:thm:manifolds} may be quoted rather than redone.

    Against that, locality interacts badly with \Cref{prob:def:PrPf}. A family of measures that is
    locally in $t$ a push-forward need not be one globally, since local representatives agree only
    in law on overlaps; so imposing a sheaf condition would force
    $\mathsf{P}(\mathcal{X})^{\Omega_n}$ to be replaced by its sheafification, a possibly larger class whose new
    members are exactly the families with no global representative. The multiplication survives
    that change --- run the argument of \Cref{prob:thm:mult} on each member of the cover --- but
    \Cref{prob:thm:representation}, which is the point of the construction, does not. Locality is
    therefore not a neutral addition here.
<!-- end rem-23 -->
<!-- rem-24: body_md -->
\label{disc:rem:one-object}
    The family $\left \{ \Omega_n\right \} _{n\ge0}$ is the product closure of $\left \{ \Omega_0,\Omega_1\right \} $, and one may ask
    whether it can be replaced by a single self-absorbing object $E\times\Omega$ with
    $E\times E\cong E$, so that the site becomes a one-object category and
    \Cref{sec:sss} becomes a rerun of \Cref{sec:qus} with $\Omega$ replaced by
    $E\times\Omega$. Both natural candidates work formally --- the Fr\'echet space $\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$
    absorbs products by interleaving, exactly as $\Omega$ does, and the colimit $\mathbb{R}^{(\mathbb{N})}$ is
    conservative over the present site --- but each carries a cost. For $\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$ the plot family is
    strictly richer than the tower, since smoothness on a Fr\'echet space is not detected on
    finite-dimensional slices, and one inherits the apparatus of convenient calculus \cite{KM97}.
    For $\mathbb{R}^{(\mathbb{N})}$ the reduction to the tower requires plots to factor locally through finite
    stages, hence a locality condition, which \Cref{disc:rem:locality} argues against. We keep the
    tower; every proof above is uniform in $n$, so it costs nothing.
<!-- end rem-24 -->
